title: Explain, Then Forget: Recommendation Unlearning under Asymmetric Access Constraint
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. Accepted ICDM 2025 (IEEE International Conference on Data Mining)
summary: Recommendation unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific historical interactions that should no longer affect future recommendations, such as noisy clicks or outdated user preferences. However, performing recommendation unlearning becomes much harder in modern Machine-Learning-as-a-Service (MLaaS) architectures, where the recommendation model is remotely hosted by a model provider (MP) and accessed by service operators (SO) only through APIs. In this setting, a service operator serves end users but cannot access or modify internal model parameters. As a result, existing unlearning methods are difficult to apply because they require access to model internals for retraining, fine-tuning, or other parameter updates. To address these challenges, we propose Causal Explanation-based Unlearning (CEU), a novel unlearning framework tailored for MLaaS environments. Instead of modifying internal model weights, CEU operates through a two-step output-level score intervention. First, it estimates how the forgotten interaction causally contributes to the current recommendation. Second, guided by this causal signal, the system removes the influence of the forgotten interaction by adjusting the final ranking scores of affected items. Because CEU leaves model parameters untouched, it naturally supports continuous unlearning requests while avoiding the error accumulation that can result from repeated parameter updates. Extensive experiments on three public datasets show that CEU achieves unlearning effectiveness comparable to full retraining while preserving recommendation utility and significantly reducing computational cost. The source code is available at: https://github.com/zhang-haichao/Explain-and-Forget.

title: Adversarial Wronskians: A proof of the Kung--Traub conjecture
summary: We prove the Kung--Traub conjecture: a deterministic stationary root-finding method without memory, using at most $n$ real scalar function or derivative evaluations per iteration, cannot have local order greater than $2^{n-1}$ on every real analytic function with a simple zero. For $n\geq2$, the bound is attained by the methods of Kung and Traub. The local estimate is required at every sufficiently close starting point, with constants that may depend on the function. Evaluation points and derivative orders may be chosen adaptively, and the rules for choosing them and processing the data are unrestricted. The proof uses a localisation property of polynomial Wronskians to obtain a lower bound at each fixed scale. A diagonal construction then gives one entire function, with derivative bounded above and below on the real line, for which every larger order fails. We also obtain a sharper bound when evaluations are made in prescribed groups, and prove the corresponding result for complex scalar evaluations. The results of this paper are also formally verified in Lean.

title: DotSpace: A New Kind of Network for People and Their Agents
summary: We introduce DotSpace, a network paradigm in which people and their agents participate as first-class members. Participants interact in persistent shared spaces, forming relationships, exchanging knowledge and taking action across ownership boundaries, while each owner retains authority over their own agents. In such a network, relationships can become channels for coordinated action: people and their agents share context, make decisions, create things and maintain ongoing commitments together, while their agents carry the work forward between people's visits. Our central proposition is that persistent networks of people and their agents can widen access to distributed capabilities and support increasingly complex collective activity. Over time, such networks may become environments in which knowledge, practices and capabilities develop, shaping both what participants can accomplish and how they organize their activity together.

title: Cutting out the middleman? Elon Musk and the rhetoric of citizen journalism in platform-mediated communication
summary: This article examines how Elon Musk constructed discourse about journalism and the media on X between the 2024 United States presidential election and Donald Trump's presidential inauguration. It investigates how references to journalism, media organisations, and platform-based communication were articulated within Musk's posts, and how users responded to these narratives during a period of intense political polarisation. The study combines computational classification, qualitative thematic coding, and inferential statistical analysis. A corpus of 2,906 posts published by Musk between 5 November 2024 and 20 January 2025 was compiled. From this corpus, 500 posts referring to journalism, media organisations, platforms, or media-related discourse were identified through AI-assisted filtering and subsequent manual review. In addition, 42,066 user responses were analysed from a stratified sample drawn from 3,233,112 interactions. The analysis examined patterns of agreement and disagreement with Musk's stance and their relationship with thematic, gender, and professional variables inferred from publicly available profile information. The findings show that Musk's discourse is organised around three recurrent dynamics: criticism of institutional journalism, the association of media organisations with political and ideological agendas, and the presentation of X as an alternative communicative space. Journalism is predominantly framed through accusations of bias, disinformation, propaganda, and electoral manipulation, whereas X is more often linked to participation, innovation, and direct communication. User responses largely converged with Musk's position, although disagreement remained visible. While thematic orientation and professional background showed statistically significant associations with agreement patterns, effect sizes were limited.

title: CausalGrade: Evidence-Guided Causal Graph Scoring with Jev
summary: Evaluating the structural quality of candidate causal graphs when the true causal structure is unknown is an important problem in applying causal discovery results. This paper proposes CausalGrade, a causal graph scoring method based on the probabilistic judgment model Jev. The method jointly provides Jev with evidence of association, conditional dependence, and directionality from observational data and edge probabilities produced by the causal discovery foundation model CDFM. Jev produces probabilistic judgments about direct causal edges, and a graph-level score is obtained by measuring the agreement between the adjacency structure of the graph under evaluation and these edge-level judgments. Across 300 synthetic datasets, the score exhibits a relatively strong negative correlation with structural error in all 20 combinations of four causal discovery algorithms and five variable counts, indicating that higher scores generally correspond to smaller structural errors. In 500 synthetic graph selection tasks, CausalGrade achieves a best-candidate hit rate of 54.4\%, exceeding the 48.4\% achieved by the Self-Compatibility metric \(κ_G\), further supporting its ability to discriminate the structural quality of graphs under evaluation.

title: Optimal Sampling and Noise Mitigation for Vocal Fold Kinematics in High-Speed Videoendoscopy
comment: This is the preprint Auhors manuscript to be published in Journal of Voice
summary: Objectives: High-Speed Videoendoscopy glottal area waveforms conflate lateral fold excursion with longitudinal opening, precluding direct estimation of velocity, acceleration, and left-right asymmetry. Displacement waveforms preserve these quantities but are susceptible to spatial quantization and temporal sampling errors. We characterize these errors, evaluate reduction via Kalman smoothing and temporal interpolation, and determine optimal frame rate bounds relative to pixel excursion, speed quotient (SQ), and open quotient (OQ). Methods: Sampling theory was used to derive analytical frame-rate bounds required for kinematic feature fidelity. Kalman smoothing was compared with FFT-based denoising, paired with sinc or spline interpolation. Interpolation was evaluated on 4000 fps recordings (N=55) downsampled and reconstructed. A 16000 fps dataset (N=12) served as reference for noise reduction across 2000-8000 fps downsampled waveforms evaluated on peak displacement, velocity, OQ, and SQ. Results: Sinc interpolation yielded lower median mean absolute error than spline (0.29 vs 0.52 pixels), with 85% of recordings (47/55) versus 45% (25/55) below 0.5 pixels. For kinematic feature estimation (N=12), Kalman-sinc outperformed FFT-sinc in 75% of feature-by-frame-rate pairings. Conclusion: Computing kinematic features without artifacts requires joint consideration of temporal and spatial resolution. Kalman-sinc preprocessing at 8000 fps is recommended for velocity and SQ measures. Peak lateral displacement can be measured at 2000 fps, while OQ requires 4000 fps for typical spatial resolutions (9-14 pixels maximum excursion). Pixel excursion should be reported alongside kinematic measures to contextualize data reliability.

title: Dual-Corrected Stochastic Block Model ($\text{DC}^2\text{SBM}$): A Generalized Structure Detection Method for Attributed Networks
summary: Community detection in attributed networks is one of the core tasks of complex network analysis. The stochastic block model (SBM) and its variants are able to detect generalized network structures such as assortative, disassortative and mixed structures. However, existing generative methods either ignore node heterogeneity, or characterize node activity in the topological and attribute dimensions by one and the same factor, making it difficult to correctly model node activity when the two kinds of activity are decoupled. In this paper, we propose the Dual-Corrected Stochastic Block Model ($\text{DC}^2\text{SBM}$), which introduces independent correction factors---a topological degree factor and an attribute abundance factor---into the link-generation and attribute-generation channels, respectively, thereby effectively decoupling node activity from membership inference, and which further introduces a global scaling parameter to resolve the mismatch between the normalization constraints and the network scale. The model is inferred by the expectation--maximization (EM) algorithm, and the newly introduced factors cancel out completely in the posterior computation, so that no additional computational cost is incurred. Experiments on synthetic and real attributed networks show that DC^2SBM outperforms state-of-the-art methods in community detection accuracy, with an especially pronounced advantage when the topological signal is weak. The two correction factors can be recovered independently from their respective channels without cross-talk. Analytical as well as controlled experiments further demonstrate that modeling with a single shared factor fails when the two kinds of activity are decoupled---a regime that is prevalent in real networks---thereby validating the necessity of dual independent correction.

title: The Geometry of Multitask Learning: Sharp Rates for Shared Subspace Estimation
summary: Learning a shared subspace in multitask learning is an important statistical problem, yet exact rates remain poorly understood in many of the formal settings considered in the literature. To address this gap, which arises from limitations of existing upper-bound techniques, we propose a general multitask lemma. The lemma provides sufficient conditions for fast subspace estimation in generic multitask settings, in the form of geometric conditions on the task regression functions and their estimators. We subsequently show that the multitask lemma yields sharp minimax rates---previously unknown---for linear regression and classification in the regimes considered, and rates matching up to logarithmic factors for additive-noise regression.

title: CalibCause: A Quality-Gated, Interpretable and Calibrated Deep Learning Framework for Diabetic Retinopathy Grading
summary: Most deep learning systems for diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading are evaluated on a single data source, with limited evidence of cross-site generalisation, uncertainty calibration, and interpretability. We propose CalibCause, a quality-gated mixture-of-experts framework that combines per-expert visual explanations, label-free image-quality conditioning, knowledge distillation, and calibrated confidence with deferral. We evaluated the framework using 51,310 fundus images from EyePACS, DDR, and APTOS 2019, with IDRiD and DeepDRiD for external testing. Evaluation included pooled testing, leave-one-environment-out experiments, paired bootstrap confidence intervals, and local grade-threshold adaptation. On the pooled test split, the label-free distilled student achieved quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.863 and accuracy of 0.865 with 27.8 million parameters, 52% fewer than its teacher. Across held-out environments, the label-free model achieved mean QWK of 0.741 compared with 0.743 for a plain ConvNeXt-Tiny baseline, while adversarial invariance did not improve cross-site grading accuracy. Refitting grade thresholds using 200 labelled images increased held-out EyePACS QWK from 0.533 to 0.621 for the label-free model. After vector scaling, expected calibration error ranged from 0.025 to 0.036 across CalibCause variants, and deferring the least confident 20% of images increased student accuracy from 0.865 to 0.923 on the remaining images. These findings demonstrate that quality-aware grading, interpretable expert routing, model compression, and calibrated deferral can be integrated without sacrificing cross-site performance relative to a plain baseline, although reliable deployment still requires local validation and adaptation.

title: Asymmetric Decline Rather Than Backfire: A Repost-Network Analysis of Japanese Vaccine-Shedding Misinformation on X
summary: This study investigates the diffusion of vaccine-shedding discourse on X in 2024, focusing on polarization in repost networks and reactions to corrective information. Here, "shedding" refers to the scientifically unsupported claim that harmful substances are released from individuals vaccinated against COVID-19 and cause adverse health effects in nearby unvaccinated people. Using 109,170 posts containing the Japanese term for "shedding" and 478,089 reposts collected from January 1 to December 31, 2024, we constructed a post-level repost network, identified discourse clusters, and examined changes in repost participation before and after major events. The results show that shedding discourse formed a two-pole structure consisting of pro-vaccine and anti-vaccine clusters. After news coverage denying shedding, we found no evidence of diffusion-level backfire in anti-vaccine repost activity. Instead, although the overall topic declined, repost participation in the anti-vaccine cluster decreased more sharply than that in the pro-vaccine cluster. User transition analysis further suggests that this change was not driven by the conversion of strongly anti-vaccine users, but by the entry of previously non-expressive users into pro-vaccine diffusion and the withdrawal of anti-vaccine supporters from repost activity. These findings suggest that corrective information may reshape the composition of misinformation diffusion participants without necessarily converting core opponents.

title: INLA for Adaptive UAV Sampling of Radio Environment Maps in IoT Networks: Prior Width Governs Accuracy and Calibration
summary: We study adaptive UAV sampling for radio environment map (REM) construction from non-Gaussian IoT observations. Integrated nested Laplace approximation(INLA) updates a Matérn GMRF posterior, with waypoints selected by entropy pre-screening and Sherman--Morrison lookahead over the reachable set. We show that the likelihood-induced Skew-Normal correction has a sextic entropy effect, explaining its limited influence on waypoint selection. Across 19 retained ray-traced windows,Random and lawnmower sampling cost a median 18.0\% and 14.0\% more residual NMSE than posterior-informed sampling, equivalently reductions of 15.3\% and 12.3\% when referred to those baselines, while differences among informative rules remain unresolved. Widening the prior shadowing standard deviation from 6.0 to 10.025\,dB improves NMSE and credible-interval coverage, with monotone improvement over a 4--16\,dB sweep on this corpus and no observed turning point, although overconfidence persists. Online width estimation from the UAV's own counts yields about 6.5\,dB without recovering the gain. Across 30 measured LoRaWAN propagation windows paired with simulated counts and scored only on received cells, the margin over non-adaptive sampling reproduces, the training-derived width minimizes the tested interval score, and GP-UCB has nominally $3$--$5\%$ lower NMSE. The results show substantial, corpus-dependent sensitivity to prior specification, while fine differences among acquisition rules have limited or unresolved effects, the preferred width depends on the corpus, scored cells and model mismatch.

title: Anchored Fusion for Automated Airway Segmentation in Pediatric and Adult CT
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Code, weights and web application: https://github.com/quin-med-harvard-edu/airway-seg
summary: Airway segmentation from chest CT enables branch-level measurement of airway size and growth, but peripheral bronchi remain hard to segment, particularly in children, whose airways are smaller and for whom few annotated scans exist. Different models recover complementary branches of the airway tree. Their union improves overall tree coverage but also introduces disconnected non-airway objects. We propose anchored fusion (A-Fuse), which takes the voxel-wise union of TfeNet, a retrained MEDPSeg and a reimplemented AirMorph and retains the connected component with greatest overlap with the AirMorph mask. On 30 held-out adult CTs from the ATM'26 training set, A-Fuse reaches a Dice score of 93.24% and the highest branch detection rate among compared methods (92.05%). On nine pediatric scans, it reaches 94.15% Dice and 68.79% branch detection. A-Fuse retains the airway tree in all 39 test scans, whereas keeping the largest component selects a non-airway object in four. A-Fuse is deployed as an automated web application and we release all code, trained weights and an open-source ITK-SNAP extension for 3D tubular segmentation editing.

title: Urban Mobility and Demand Dynamics: A Telemetry and Ticketing Baseline for Niteroi's Bus Network
comment: 6 pages, 7 figures, paper was peer-reviewed and presented at NetMob 2026 (Data Challenge Track)
summary: The public transportation networks of rapidly expanding urban centers confront a complex task in balancing operational efficiency with dynamic commuter needs. In response, data-driven approaches leveraging multi-perspective datasets offer critical insights into a city's systemic demand. In this work, we utilize the NetMob 2026 Data Challenge dataset for the city of Niteroi, Brazil, to investigate the structural dynamics of the municipal bus network. Specifically, our research framework is driven by three interconnected urban mobility objectives: first, analyzing urban movement patterns to determine whether passenger boarding logs trace periodic, routine, and predictable movement patterns across distinct urban zones; second, detecting operational anomalies and potential bottlenecks by analyzing vehicle trajectory profiles via GPS telemetry to identify both scheduled and unscheduled stops; and third, developing and evaluating a supervised learning framework capable of predicting continuous bus trip durations.

title: Model-Agnostic Search for New Physics in the Presence of Imperfect Background by Smearing the Data
summary: In the search for new particles in high-energy physics, it is necessary to first define the signal region (SR) enriched in signal events, and then compare events in this region with the expected background distribution. While most existing search methods rely on prior domain knowledge of either the signal or the background, there has been less effort to relax both assumptions simultaneously, as methods that weaken one assumption typically rely on strong knowledge of the other. We propose Model-Agnostic Search with Smearing and Imperfect Background (MASSIB), a method that addresses this challenge by learning the density ratio of events relative to a misspecified background distribution using modern tools from machine learning, and defining the SR as the region with high density ratio. Recognizing that a naive application of this idea introduces significant bias in background estimation when interpolating from the control region to the SR, MASSIB mitigates this issue by introducing a "smeared" density ratio, which can be learned efficiently through data-level manipulation and used to define an SR that allows for accurate background estimation. By applying it to various types of simulated Large Hadron Collider (LHC) events with realistic background mismodeling, we demonstrate that MASSIB identifies a data-driven SR that achieves high signal concentration consistently across different types of signals while avoiding bias in background estimation. The method does this without making strong assumptions about either the signal or background distribution. We then show that this robustness extends to the validity and strong statistical power of the resulting hypothesis tests for signal detection, demonstrating the potential of this approach for future model-agnostic searches at the LHC.

title: DiffUltra: Task-Guided Pathology Synthesis for Large-Scale Real-World Lung Ultrasound Data
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Despite their scale, large medical imaging datasets may underrepresent clinically relevant pathological presentations. Synthetic data can expand coverage, but findings must remain compatible with surrounding anatomy. This is challenging in ultrasound, where findings resemble surrounding tissue and must be positioned relative to anatomical landmarks. We propose DiffUltra, a task-guided latent diffusion pipeline that models pathological structure and spatial context, and screens synthetic images for downstream utility. DiffUltra conditions generation on structural masks decomposing findings into anechoic, hypoechoic, and hyperechoic subregions. Two placement strategies insert findings into pathology-absent backgrounds or replace existing findings with structurally matched pathology from other patients. A filter trained exclusively on real data retains images whose predictions agree spatially with target boxes. We evaluate DiffUltra for lung ultrasound detection of pleural effusion and consolidation, using over 700,000 expert-annotated frames from 598 patients at 12 sites. Averaged across three real-data scales, synthetic insertion significantly improved video-level AUROC for both pleural effusion (p = 0.017) and consolidation (p < 0.01). For pleural effusion, frame-level average precision improved by 4.5 percentage points on average and by 6.1 points using only 10% of real data (p < 0.01 for both). Synthetic insertion also yielded larger average precision gains than an existing diffusion-based lesion-insertion method at every scale. At full scale, targeted synthesis improved AUROC for both pathologies by 1.1-3.9 points in an underrepresented anatomical zone and on a held-out acquisition system. These results suggest that anatomically constrained, task-guided synthesis can help address coverage gaps in ultrasound training data.

title: JYVA at BeTraC: Audio-Based Medical Note Generation with SOAP Section-Specific Queries
summary: We present our submission to the Beyond Transcription Challenge (BeTraC) on medical note generation from doctor-patient audio conversations. We propose a section-aware approach based on Qwen2.5-Omni-3B, in which a lightweight Q-Former learns SOAP section-specific queries to extract compact clinical representations from speech. In the lightweight track, our system ranks fourth and substantially outperforms the challenge baseline, achieving a Concept F1 of 0.5005 on the official test set. The organizers' analysis and our heuristic evaluation suggest improved robustness to hallucinations, and better stability under difficult audio conditions. These results show that explicitly modeling SOAP structure through section-specific queries is an effective way to improve the faithfulness and reliability of audio-based medical note generation.

title: Robust-by-Design Distributional Learning from Contaminated Samples
summary: Modern data analysis pipelines increasingly rely on large datasets assembled through retrieval, scraping, automated filtering, and post-hoc curation, where the observed sample is often a contaminated mixture rather than the target population. Standard distributional objectives either ignore contamination and converge to the wrong target, or retain only a small trusted subset and discard most of the data. We study supervised and unsupervised learning when a clean reference sample is compared with a pooled sample from $r=(1-ε)q+εz$, where $q$ is the latent target distribution and $z$ is an unknown contaminant. Motivated by settings with noisy membership scores for all observations and exact labels for a small audited subset, we propose contamination-corrected maximum mean discrepancy (CC-MMD), a design-based estimator that combines proxy scores with audited residual corrections to recover the oracle MMD that would have been computed from the latent clean sample. CC-MMD requires no calibration assumption on the proxy scores and no structural assumptions on the contaminant beyond standard kernel regularity. We prove finite-population design-unbiasedness of the corrected kernel sums, establish asymptotic normality of the audit correction, and show consistency for the target discrepancy $\mathrm{MMD}^2(p,q;k)$. Empirically, CC-MMD tracks the oracle under increasing contamination, improves parameter recovery and prediction in contaminated regression, and enables generative models trained on heavily corrupted mixtures to recover the clean target distribution. These results show that contaminated data need not be discarded or treated as the estimand. With sparse trusted labels and abundant noisy supervision, distributional objectives can be made robust by design.

title: TheseusSyn: Unified Medical Image Synthesis via Context-Conditioned Masked Autoregression
summary: High-fidelity medical image synthesis is promising for data-efficient learning and privacy-preserving model development. However, most existing approaches rely on symbolic or label-based conditioning, which constrains generative diversity and limits case-specific contextual fidelity. Inspired by the Ship of Theseus paradox, we propose TheseusSyn, a novel context-conditioned synthesis paradigm that generates images through iterative content replacement. Our framework employs a multi-codebook discrete tokenizer to convert medical images into sequences of token indices, extracted with a global representation token that serves as a contextual constraint. A masked autoregressive generative model then iteratively masks and predicts tokens conditioned on both local neighborhoods and the global context. By progressively replacing image content until the entire token sequence is renewed, TheseusSyn produces synthetic samples that preserve anatomical coherence and semantic consistency while introducing controlled diversity. We evaluate the proposed framework on multiple datasets from MedMNIST by constructing synthetic datasets with varying masking strategies and training ResNet-18 classifiers exclusively on either real or synthetic data. Experimental results demonstrate that classifiers trained on TheseusSyn-generated images achieve competitive performance on official test sets, indicating that the synthesized data preserve diagnostically relevant features and semantic consistency. Systematic analysis of masking strategies reveals their impact on structural fidelity and downstream classification accuracy. These results suggest that context-conditioned masked autoregression provides an effective and generalizable solution for label-free medical image synthesis, offering a scalable alternative to conventional data augmentation and class-conditioned generative models in medical imaging applications.

title: Automatic Construction of Strong Simple Baselines
summary: To rigorously establish the value of a novel deep learning method, it must be compared against appropriate baselines. As deep learning has become increasingly common in the physical and life sciences, there have been numerous cases in which apparent progress has turned out to be an artifact of omitted or missing baselines. In this work, we investigate whether this problem can be mitigated by using large language models to automate the construction of baselines. We assemble 36 supervised classification and regression tasks from peer-reviewed studies in Nature, Science, and Cell-family journals that investigate novel deep learning methods for scientific applications. We then use a language model to construct simple baselines for each task. These automatically constructed baselines are strong, recovering a median of 95.5% (mean 85.7%) of the gap between a trivial predictor and the score of the deep learning model. The median simple baseline matches or exceeds the performance of the deep learning model in 12 studies. We further examine the variation across scientific domains and publication venues and we characterize the effects of test-time compute and access to different levels of study context. As human peer review has struggled to keep up with the rapidly increasing volume of research articles in recent years, our results suggest that automated baseline construction is a practical and scalable check on deep learning contributions in the physical and life sciences.

title: Global Testing of Gaussian Means by Combining Marginal and Conditional Evidence
summary: We propose a test of the global null hypothesis of zero means in correlated multivariate Gaussian data by combining marginal and conditional evidence at each coordinate. The conditional tests are based on the distribution of each coordinate given the remaining coordinates. At each coordinate, the corresponding two-sided $p$-values are combined using the Simes method, followed by a Bonferroni correction across coordinates. Because conditioning can either strengthen or weaken evidence against the null, neither marginal nor conditional testing is uniformly preferable. The proposed procedure adapts to their relative strengths while retaining the simplicity of minimum-type global testing. We establish finite-sample control of the global Type-I error under both known covariance and covariance estimated from an independent sample. The latter setting requires a careful analysis of the dependence between studentized marginal and conditional statistics. We evaluate the power of the proposed test through simulations, compare its performance with existing global tests, and illustrate its practical utility using a TCGA carcinoma dataset.

title: Report-Derived Labels, an Image Teacher and the Gap to Expert Labels in Knee MRI: An Analysis of One Entry to the RSNA 2026 Knee Abnormality Detection Challenge
summary: In the RSNA 2026 Knee Abnormality Detection challenge, 58 of 4,407 training studies have expert labels for 12 findings, and the rest have only a radiology report. We compare training targets built from a language-model reading of the reports and from a public image model against two references: the expert labels and the 39,248 study-finding cells that the reports state as present or absent. The report labels and the out-of-fold predictions of the image model reach similar agreement with the expert labels (macro AUC 0.892 and 0.896) but fail on different findings. The report is better for ligament tears and patellofemoral osteoarthritis, which it never calls present when the experts do not; the image model is better for effusion, Baker's cyst, contusion, and synovitis, where the reports call the finding absent, leave it out, or call it present more often than the experts. Their equal mixture reaches 0.927 (gain over the report labels 0.035, 95% interval 0.019 to 0.052), also after removing the studies whose knee side was handled inconsistently. We did not observe a model-level gain from this better target: a 2.5D ResNet50 trained on the report labels alone scored 0.877 on the private leaderboard, after the deadline, against 0.872 for the same model trained on the mixture, and the out-of-fold advantage of the mixture is confounded by a change of code and by possible leakage through the image model's folds. A scanner prevalence prior raised agreement with the reports but not with the experts, so a report-derived reference can reward reporting habits. A rank correction for co-occurring findings gave small out-of-fold gains and no visible leaderboard effect. Our entry, a forked public ensemble with that correction, was displayed at rank 582 of 6,299 on the private leaderboard (0.943, a score shared by 287 teams). All results are exploratory; none of the models is meant for clinical use.

title: FGSM Attack Transferability from Simulation to Quantum Hardware in Network Intrusion Detection
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE 2nd International Conference on Quantum Artificial Intelligence (QAI), 13-16 December 2026, Nottingham, UK. Code: https://github.com/xeeshanajmal/qai2026-fgsm-transfer
summary: Quantum computers are now available through cloud platforms, and recent work has proposed using them to detect network intrusions. It is not yet clear how easily such systems can be attacked. We train a hybrid variational quantum classifier (VQC) on the Friday DDoS subset of CICIDS2017 and test it against two attacks: label flipping during training and FGSM evasion at prediction time. We run the tests in simulation and on IBM hardware, the Fez superconducting processor (Heron r2). We find that two models with similar accuracy can differ greatly in how easily they are attacked. A model that decides with little confidence loses half its detections to a very small change in the input, while a model trained to decide with more confidence needs a much larger change before it fails. Attacks built in simulation against the more confident model also work on real hardware, and the device classifies every unaltered attack sample correctly. Simulated device noise does not reduce accuracy, but it does reduce the model's confidence and makes attacks easier, so accuracy alone does not show how exposed a model is. Label flipping has no measurable effect until 15% of attack labels are changed. These results show that device noise should not be treated as a defense and that reported weaknesses in these classifiers depend partly on how they were trained.

title: Quantum amplification of improbable futures
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables, 4 supplementary tables, graphical abstract
summary: Some consequential futures consist of entirely plausible steps arranged into an unlikely sequence, such as ordinary weather anomalies combining into an extreme event or local equipment failures propagating into a widespread outage. Because the sequence as a whole carries little probability, it may be rarely observed in simulation. Quantum mechanics offers a way to change those odds: ideal amplitude amplification raises the chance of drawing such futures while preserving their relative likelihoods. For a five-state process six steps ahead, 13,888 of 15,625 futures are rare, yet together they account for about one draw in 40. We built the complete circuit in IBM's Qiskit and checked every part against an exact enumeration; four simulated rounds raised the share of rare futures drawn from 2.5% to 98.0%. On IBM's Kingston quantum computer, a two-step reference circuit that marks rare futures from a precomputed list drew them in 68.4% of shots against 43.5% for its control (z = 50); at three steps (about 1,170 two-qubit gates) the predicted signal reversed sign. Because this model's probabilities are known, every result could be checked against exact values; the mechanism is intended for simulators whose probabilities are hard to calculate, such as climate, epidemic and financial models.

title: Cross-Device Transfer of a Hospital-Trained Fetal Head Circumference Model to a Low-Cost Handheld Ultrasound Probe
summary: Automated fetal head circumference (HC) measurement reaches near-expert accuracy on the HC18 benchmark, but published models are trained and evaluated on hospital-grade equipment. We quantify what happens when such a model is carried to a low-cost handheld probe. A lightweight segmentation network (CSM, 0.13M parameters) was trained on HC18 across five independent runs and applied without modification to images from a $1,350 handheld probe (SonoQue C3), acquired at the same visit as the reference hospital scan in 18 patients. In-domain accuracy was 2.34 +/- 0.43 mm; on handheld images the same model gave 16.12 mm against the hospital record, a 6.9-fold degradation. Input preprocessing, a choice rarely reported, accounted for about a third of that gap: direct resizing gave 49.45 mm against 16.12 mm for an aspect-preserving pipeline. A leave-one-out data-efficiency curve showed that fine-tuning on two images significantly worsened accuracy, and that from four images upward error fell by 0.75 mm per doubling of the local dataset (p = 0.0045), although no training-set size up to 27 images significantly improved on the unmodified model. Much of the residual gap belongs to the reference rather than the model: scored against a manual tracing of the same image the model was already within 10.48 mm, and its disagreement with sonographer calipers on the same frame was a near-constant offset, negative in 10 of 10 cases. A single calibration constant estimated leave-one-out reduced that disagreement from 8.12 mm to 3.49 mm, reaching the intraobserver reproducibility reported for experienced sonographers, but did not improve agreement with the hospital record. Cross-device evaluations should therefore report the input preprocessing used and characterise the precision of their reference standard.

title: PrivacyFlow: Privacy in AI Agents through Information Flow Analysis and Consequence-Aware Risk Management
summary: Autonomous LLM agents executing multi-step workflows over personal data often misalign with user privacy expectations and leak sensitive, out-of-context information. Although Contextual Integrity (CI) formalizes this problem, existing benchmarks and defenses rarely operationalize CI for realistic multi-step task sequences in evolving environments. In this work, we first introduce agentic PrivacyBench, a benchmark of 5873 tasks in 986 task sequences with dynamic environment updates and CI-grounded allow-sets for sensitive information. We also introduce PrivacyFlow, a defense that separates deliberative privacy planning (System 2) from task execution (System 1), treating each sharing decision as a structured risk-management problem. Before execution, PrivacyFlow traces the provenance and purpose of each planned data flow, models recipient background knowledge, and simulates what external actors could infer. This allows us to model the downstream consequences of disclosure, including inference attacks and context-dependent harms. It then weighs the remaining disclosure risk against task utility and executes a minimized plan, blocks it, or consults the user. Across six models, PrivacyFlow significantly reduces step-level privacy failures and raises the share of completed task sequences without a detected privacy violation by 22--55 percentage points. We further highlight a new privacy--utility--autonomy tradeoff: allowing PrivacyFlow to proactively prompt the user in case of uncertainty can increase authorized task completion at the cost of shifting decision effort back to the user. Our results suggest that proactive CI reasoning can substantially improve agentic privacy and motivate further study of this tradeoff.

title: Approximate Bayesian Fusion
summary: Distributed inference plays an important role in modern computational statistics and machine learning. In the frequentist setting, methods can often aggregate results by simply averaging estimators computed on data subsets. However, distributed Bayesian inference is more challenging, as it requires reconstructing the full posterior by combining subposterior distributions computed on different machines. Bayesian Fusion performs distributed Bayesian inference exactly, but at a sizeable computational cost. We propose a method that uses numerical approximations to reduce the cost of the most computationally expensive steps of Bayesian Fusion, and expands its domain of applicability. We bound the numerical error as a function of the step size of the approximation. Under regularity conditions, our approach can approximate the target posterior distribution to an arbitrary degree of accuracy, and is a practical and efficient alternative for large-scale distributed Bayesian inference. In numerical experiments on a logistic regression with more than $300{,}000$ observations, our method reaches the accuracy reported for Divide-and-Conquer Bayesian Fusion about two orders of magnitude faster. On a proportional hazards model with non-Gaussian posteriors, which lacks the lower bounds that Bayesian Fusion requires, our method reproduces funnel features of the posterior that simpler methods like Consensus Monte Carlo miss.

title: CS-LDM: Clinically Guided Structure-Aware Latent Diffusion for Knee Radiographic Forecasting
summary: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a leading cause of physical disability and currently has no curative clinical treatment. Early diagnosis and accurate prognosis are therefore vital for managing its progression. Existing methods mainly predict future severity grades and provide limited visual explanation of structural change. Recent generation-guided approaches synthesize follow-up radiographs for progression assessment, but generated images are often judged by predictive accuracy or image realism, so they may satisfy a grading model while remaining morphologically unreliable. We therefore propose CS-LDM, a clinically guided, structure-aware latent diffusion framework that forecasts patient-specific future knee radiographs from the current X-ray and clinically available current KL grade, using LoRA adaptation, current-grade conditioning, and frozen-teacher diagnostic distillation. Experiments on the public Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) dataset show that CS-LDM improves future severity-grade consistency while maintaining competitive image fidelity. Further ordinal, OARSI, ROI-level, and stable/progressed analyses show that radiographic forecasting should be evaluated by balancing diagnostic consistency, anatomical plausibility, and structural preservation.

title: Characterizing LLM Agent Behaviors in Module Shadowing Environments
summary: LLM agents operating in untrusted workspaces face the risk of untrusted code execution during routine tasks, yet final reports and workspace states alone cannot reliably establish whether execution occurred. We introduce an evaluation framework that codes observation, reasoning, execution, and response behaviors from agent trajectories and aligns them with independent environmental records to reconstruct execution histories and verify final reports. We apply this framework to module shadowing, in which a local file is loaded in place of a trusted module during import, enabling untrusted code execution without adversarial prompts. Across 90 trials with 15 models, the payload executed in 51% of direct shadowing trials and 87% of indirect shadowing trials. Even explicit recognition of the shadowing mechanism did not ensure prevention, as the payload ran in 10 of the 29 trials with recorded recognition. These failures were often omitted from final reports, as 49 of the 62 triggered trials ended without mention of the security issue. Three reports even denied execution, including one from a trial in which independent logs recorded 19 payload executions. Final workspace states also obscured prior execution when agents deleted or overwrote the payload marker in 10 triggered trials. These findings demonstrate that combining behavioral coding with independent environmental auditing enables rigorous and transparent evaluation of agent safety.

title: What Paid Triangles Identify about Reserve Uncertainty: Information Boundaries in Loss Reserving
comment: 69 pages (main text 32 pages, supplementary material pp. 33-69), 1 figure, 27 tables. R code: https://github.com/robin-vo/hgr
summary: Paid triangles identify some components of reserve uncertainty while others enter through modelling assumptions. We distinguish population identification, recovery by free accident-year-level and two-stage second-moment fits, and precision at practical triangle sizes. In a compound frequency--severity hierarchy, the population law identifies the row dispersion governing non-diversifying reserve variance. With one free level per accident year, its profile likelihood attains its supremum only at homogeneity: the levels absorb realised row heterogeneity on every triangle, in amounts and in counts. Anchoring reopens this channel, but supplies only one observation per accident year. On a $10 \times 10$ triangle the anchored estimate remains uncertain by a factor of several. Within-row allocation dispersion survives conditioning on row totals and hence survives free levels. In the predictive experiments, the treatment of mean-structure estimation error separated the procedures by several times more than the choice among plausible variance laws. A law of the correct form improved coverage only when its dispersion came from a prior instead of the free-level fit. On an outcome-free Schedule~P panel, no amount-only procedure approaches nominal coverage. Strongly one-sided misses reveal a displacement of realised reserves relative to the fitted predictive centres that changing the amount-only variance law cannot repair.

title: Zonal-Aware Prostate Cancer Detection and Classification via Hadamard-Fused Mamba-UNet
comment: Published in SPIE Medical Imaging - Computer-Aided Diagnosis Conference
summary: Accurate clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) detection from prostate MRI requires a detailed understanding of the prostate anatomical context. Deep learning approaches have achieved promising results in zonal and lesion segmentation; however, the joint analysis of prostate zonal anatomy and lesion morphology in a unified framework remains relatively underexplored. In this work, we propose ZH-Mamba, a multi-stage zonal-aware csPCa detection framework consisting of two H-Mamba UNets models for prostate zonal segmentation and lesion localization, followed by an anatomy-aware Convolutional Neural Network classifier for csPCa detection. The proposed model leverages a learnable Hadamard Transform-based fusion mechanism to enhance zonal and lesion feature representations without increasing computational complexity. The learned fusion patterns consistently emphasize prostate regions, suggesting that the proposed fusion captures anatomically relevant feature representations. We demonstrate a strong zonal segmentation performance on the PI-CAI dataset, reaching Dice scores of $\textbf{0.95}$, $\textbf{0.85}$, and $\textbf{0.95}$ for whole gland (WG), peripheral zone (PZ), and transition zone (TZ), respectively, providing robust anatomical priors for downstream csPCa detection. Experimental results on an independent internal dataset confirm the generalization capability of the proposed zonal segmentation model. For lesion localization, the H-Mamba UNet achieves a competitive Dice score of $\textbf{0.70}$. Integrating the zonal masks and lesion localization, the proposed ZH-Mamba framework achieves an AUC of $\textbf{0.86}$, Average Precision ($\mathrm{AP}_{\mathrm{Patient}}$) of $\textbf{0.72}$, and F1 score of $\textbf{0.76}$, demonstrating the effectiveness of zonal-aware csPCa detection.

title: MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection
summary: LLM agents are increasingly used to automate vulnerability detection, but reliable detection is challenging because agents must distinguish subtle, security-relevant fixes from benign code variation. While underlying LLM capability has improved significantly, the accuracy of the agent still depends heavily on the harness: the code that defines the scaffolding around the LLM. Harnesses are typically fixed, and largely hand-written, limiting adaptation to evaluator feedback. Additionally, when harnesses are static, improvements on one dataset or model may not transfer to others. To address these challenges, we introduce MetaVul, a self-improving framework for harness discovery in vulnerability detection. Starting from a seed structured reasoning scaffold, MetaVul uses a workflow-based optimization loop to iteratively refine the harness using feedback from paired vulnerable and patched functions, while preserving the structured reasoning and verdict format. At each iteration, it searches over the history of prior harnesses, with access to their trajectories, logs, and metrics, and it returns a set of Pareto-optimal harnesses. We apply MetaVul to discover agent harnesses for various architectures. A validation set (202 pairs) is used for optimization, while an unseen dataset (430 pairs) is kept as the held-out set. We test whether harnesses learned from one model transfer to others not seen during optimization. Results on both frontier and small LLMs show that the optimized harnesses improve pairwise vulnerability detection up to 23.3 percentage points on the validation set and up to 25.8 points on the held-out set with a Pareto-frontier harness. Harnesses learned with one model also transfer to others. We show that harnesses optimized with one model transfer to another, improving held-out pairwise accuracy by 14.7 points without further optimization.

title: Marginal effects for the stochastic actor-oriented model
comment: 91 pages (57 pages main text), 9 figures, 4 tables. Comments welcome
summary: Parameter estimates of stochastic actor-oriented models for network evolution are notoriously hard to interpret. Especially a comparison of parameter estimates is problematic, both between different models for the same data set and between the same model for different data sets. Effect size measures based on the calculation of marginal effects are proposed as an alternative to standardize the scale of interpretation but can and should not universally erase the effects of differences in scale and heterogeneity. Simulation experiments show how an omitted effect displaces coefficients and marginal effects differently, and an analysis of empirical friendship network data finds that reciprocity and triadic closure reinforce one another when ties are created but partially substitute for one another when ties are maintained, a contrast the coefficients do not reveal.

title: LAPIS: Clinically Constrained Patient-Identity Residual Learning for Chest X-Ray Anonymization
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027
summary: Biometric information in chest radiographs limits their release for research, as patients can be re-identified. We propose LAPIS, which jointly adapts a spatial chest-radiograph latent space so that patient-discriminative information concentrates in a compact, replaceable channel residual while most clinically relevant content stays in the complement. The residual is defined by an exactly semi-orthogonal basis, a spatial adversary suppresses identity leakage from the complement, and replacement-aware training teaches the decoder cross-patient residual swaps under output identity, clinical and realism constraints, so that replacing the residual yields a valid image. At release, the residual is replaced by a mixture of donor residuals. On patient-disjoint model, release and test sets from ChestX-ray14, we evaluate attackers adapted to the anonymized setting, a structural source-retrieval attack, and pathology classifiers trained on released images and tested on real ones. LAPIS reduces worst-case cross-study linkability from 0.961 to 0.791 AUC at a macro AUROC cost of 0.012 relative to reconstruction; a deformation-based baseline, however, remains better at structural source retrieval.

title: Li$^{2}$SAO: Lifting Light Singl-Rollout Asynchronous RL Optimization via Group-Relative Actor-Critic Bootstrapping
summary: Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) is becoming a mainstream paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs), as it improves training efficiency by updating the model as rollouts arrive. Recent work argues that group-wise sampling in GRPO does not naturally fit asynchronous RL training because rollout lengths follow a long-tailed distribution, and proposes Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization (SAO) to improve stability and off-policy behavior, especially on agentic tasks. However, SAO relies on a closed-source value model obtained from scaling value pretraining. In this paper, we analyze GRPO and LiSAO, our lightweight reproduction of SAO without the pretrained value model, on single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic tasks. We find that GRPO outperforms LiSAO on reasoning tasks, while the reverse holds on agentic tasks. Since the value model of LiSAO is not yet well trained , LiSAO lags behind GRPO substantially in early training steps. To address this issue, we propose Li$^{2}$SAO, which Lifts Light Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization with group-relative actor-critic bootstrapping: while the critic is cold, a group-relative advantage trains the actor and a group-centered return trains the critic, after which training switches to single-rollout GAE. Experiments show that Li$^{2}$SAO catches up with or surpasses GRPO in early training and further raises the later performance ceiling. Code is available at https://github.com/jd-cc-coder/Li2SAO.

title: Statistical inference for quantile correlation regression with bivariate outcomes
summary: It is increasing scientifically important to recognize, quantify and visualize the dependence structure between the bivariate outcomes. In this paper, we investigate conditional dependence using a new dependence measure, the quantile correlation coefficient, which is defined by the Pearson correlation of two quantile-hits of bivariate outcomes. Furthermore, we propose a new regression model for covariate effects directly on the quantile correlation coefficient via a generalized linear regression model. The proposed model has intuitive interpretation and provides a comprehensive view of covariate effects across quantiles of bivariate outcomes. The proposed estimator enjoys desirable asymptotic properties including uniform consistency and weak convergence as a process in the quantile index. Additionally, we develop the general hypothesis testing for the regression coefficients, with applications to summarize covariate effects across the quantile ranges. Simulation studies demonstrate the good finite sample performance of the proposed estimation and inference procedures. Two empirical applications of the proposed method reveal interesting insights in premature twins data for measuring association and ChIP-seq data for measuring reproducibility.

title: VoxLock: Target-Speaker Extraction for Voice Agents Without an Enrollment Step
comment: 4 pages, 4 tables. Model, code and per-file scores: https://github.com/arbazsiddiqui/voxlock
summary: A voice agent's speech recognizer transcribes everyone near the microphone, including people other than the caller. I fine-tuned a public causal target-speaker extraction model (REAL-TSE, 27M parameters) on one GPU to work from a voice sample cut from the call itself, and released it as VoxLock. I score it by what a recognizer writes on real recordings. On Krisp's 265-recording benchmark it reaches 4.95% WER against 23.21% unprocessed and lets 9 background words into the transcript over 85 minutes of background-only speech. Its WER is not significantly different from Krisp's best filters and is significantly lower than the other commercial and open systems I tested. On 400 AMI meeting windows built and frozen before scoring, it cuts WER from 42.95% to 10.63%. The 8-bit model runs a live call on 77% of one CPU thread with 24 ms of algorithmic latency. Model, code and per-file scores are open.

title: Bayesian Distribution System State Estimation with Flow Matching
summary: Medium-voltage feeders have few real-time measurements, so distribution system state estimation (DSSE) rests on pseudo-measurements of the secondary substations, a prior in Bayesian terms. Weighted least squares keeps the power flow exact but reduces this prior to a mean and variance, while supervised deep learning estimators also learn the power flow and are tied to one measurement set. We propose PoSE (posterior sampling for state estimation), which keeps the Bayesian structure of DSSE and learns only what the distribution system operator does not know, namely the distribution of substation injections, modelled by a neural network trained with flow matching on historical data. The power flow equations, grid topology and measurements enter only at sampling, through a noise-aware Kalman-type correction. The neural network therefore never approximates the power flow, but every posterior sample is a physically consistent operating point, and one trained prior serves any measurement set, noise level and topology. On the IEEE 33-bus feeder, PoSE lowers the probabilistic injection error (CRPS) by 6.7-7.5% against a full-covariance Gaussian prior in all 12 tested settings. It provides reliable uncertainty: the 90% intervals contain the true injection almost exactly as often as exact posterior samples would, whereas those of supervised estimators contain it in only 37-78% of cases. On the 240-bus unbalanced three-phase Iowa feeder, it gives the lowest injection, voltage and branch-current errors of all estimators. A fast variant matches this accuracy at 0.2-0.6s per snapshot and, without retraining, beats Gaussian priors and retrained supervised estimators on seven reconfigured topologies.

title: Adaptive Uncertainty Quantification on Simplicial Complexes with Conformalized Simplicial Neural Networks
summary: Simplicial neural networks (SNNs) are powerful tools for prediction tasks on higher-order relational datasets stored on simplicial complexes (SCs), a higher-order generalization of graphs. However, SNNs usually lack rigorous uncertainty quantification (UQ), limiting their usefulness in high-stakes scenarios. We propose conformalized SNN (CF-SNN), a framework that, given a simplicial-complex entity with m prediction targets, generates prediction sets for all m targets simultaneously. Under mild assumptions, CF-SNN guarantees that, for each target, the prediction set contains the true label with a user-specified nominal coverage probability, and the realized miscoverage proportion across all m targets is guaranteed to remain close to the nominal level with high probability. Extensive experiments across a wide range of SC prediction tasks demonstrate that CF-SNN is a flexible UQ framework that achieves user-specified coverage while producing informative prediction sets of small size.

title: Quantifying Linepack Storage Potential of Hydrogen Networks
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures, submitted to the International Journal of Hydrogen Energy
summary: Future hydrogen systems depend on large-scale storage to balance supply and demand. Hydrogen networks can store energy in the pipelines themselves, but the potential of this linepack storage has not been quantified comparably to dedicated storage facilities. We transfer metrics established for conventional storage, such as volume capacity and full-cycle equivalents, to hydrogen networks. To evaluate them, we formulate an optimization problem maximizing linepack storage utilization, subject to non-convex PDE-based constraints describing transient gas flow. We solve the optimization problem over a full-year horizon to capture seasonal variations and to assess the interaction with cavern storage. For computational tractability, we propose a simulation-informed sequential convex programming approach with adaptive time stepping that reduces problem size by up to 98% at accuracy comparable to fixed-resolution methods. For the GasLib-40 topology with German scenario data, the network provides a volume capacity of 24 million normal cubic meters at 28 full-cycle equivalents per year.

title: Don't Just Impute, Detect: Task-Aware Diffusion Pipelines for Edge Anomaly Detection
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at the 33rd IEEE International Conference on High Performance Computing, Data, and Analytics (HiPC 2026)
summary: Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) edge pipelines routinely lose contiguous blocks of multi-sensor data to network dropouts and hardware faults. The standard remedy is a disjointed "impute-then-detect" pipeline whose imputer is trained only for Mean Squared Error (MSE). Such an imputer fills a missing block with the most probable normal pattern: a partially observed anomaly is smoothed back toward normality, and boundary artifacts on normal data raise false alarms. We call this imputation bias and propose the Task-Aware Diffusion Refiner (TADR), a conditional diffusion refiner trained against the loss landscape of a frozen downstream detector. Because back-propagating through the sampling trajectory is intractable, the task-aware terms act on the one-step clean-window estimate that the noise prediction already yields, so training costs no more than plain diffusion training. Under strict Point-to-Point evaluation over five seeds with paired significance tests, TADR raises F1 by $0.338$ over the unrefined detector on SMD ($p = 0.0015$), and the anomaly enhancement objective alone contributes $0.463$ in ablation. We also characterise when the method helps: the gain tracks the continuous, mutually redundant channels available and the anomaly evidence the outage removes, and it is absent on telemetry datasets dominated by one-hot command channels and on PSM. At ten sampling steps TADR runs in $41.4$ ms per window on a single CPU core, sustaining about $24$ concurrent 1 Hz streams from a $4.03$ MB model. Code and per-seed results are available at https://github.com/int-park422/TADR.

title: Balancing Covariates for Continuous Treatments by Exploiting Continuity
summary: We consider causal effect estimation in observational studies with continuous treatment. We introduce a general class of causal estimands that, as a special case, includes the average causal effect of assigning treatment according to an arbitrary counterfactual distribution. Balancing estimators are particularly attractive tools for covariate adjustment in this setting because they avoid directly modeling the treatment assignment mechanism, thereby reducing the potential for instability and misspecification bias in subsequent causal effect estimation. In this paper, we develop a general framework of covariate balancing for continuous treatment with the proposed class of causal estimands, leveraging the assumption of continuity of treatment dose. As in the binary treatment setting, analysts specify the basis functions to be balanced, the allowable degree of covariate imbalance, and a criterion for selecting among admissible weights. Under a minimum variance criterion for choosing weights, we establish consistency, characterize the effect of basis misspecification, and prove asymptotic normality. We develop consistent variance estimation, which yields asymptotically valid confidence intervals. Under homoskedasticity, our estimator is provably more efficient than inverse probability weighting based on the \emph{true} propensity score. Simulation studies support our theoretical results, and we illustrate the proposed method by estimating the effect of vocational training hours on expected future earnings using data from the U.S. Job Corps study.

title: Joint Estimation and Network Configuration in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Distributed consensus-based sensing enables a multi-agent system to collaboratively estimate an unknown state by combining local measurements with information received from neighboring agents. In practice, however, the communication network, transmission delays, and finite-rate communication directly affect the disagreement among agents. On the other hand, agreement among agents does not ensure accuracy, particularly when sensors have different measurement uncertainties. We develop a sampled consensus-plus-innovations framework under realistic wireless network constraints that jointly accounts for inter-agent disagreement and estimation inaccuracy. We derive a computable upper bound on the worst-case steady-state estimation error that captures consensus disagreement due to the communication graph, quantization error, and transmission delay, together with estimation inaccuracy, which accounts for measurement uncertainty against the true state. We then use this bound as a network design objective and propose a semi-distributed auction-based algorithm that jointly modifies the communication graph and link-rate allocation. The proposed method preserves connectivity, converges in finite time to a locally auction-stable network configuration, and reduces the bound on the estimation error at every accepted change. The proposed method has been evaluated on various test cases, and the results show that it reduces the estimation error while maintaining fewer links and allocating moderate link rates in a short time.

title: RiskyPy: Toward Model-Calibrated Prompt Generation for Joint Security and Functionality Evaluation of LLM-Generated Code
summary: Evaluating approaches that improve the security of LLM code generation requires datasets that jointly assess security and functionality and remain adapted to the capabilities of the models being studied. However, existing benchmarks are costly to produce and are generally not calibrated to a chosen range of model capabilities. We introduce RiskyPy, an automated pipeline that generates security-oriented code-generation datasets calibrated to model proficiency using functionality and vulnerability canaries. We instantiate RiskyPy for Python using domains covering 18 CWEs from the 2025 CWE Top 25, producing 101 prompts. Experiments on Qwen3-4B and Seed-Coder-8B show that the generated tasks remain functionally accessible, with 57-72% of prompts yielding functional code, while only 5-10% of generations are free of Bandit findings, leaving room for joint evaluation of security and functionality of security improvement approaches.

title: Source projection for calibrated transfer learning in survival prediction
comment: 55 pages including supplementary material; 5 figures and 18 tables
summary: Transfer learning can improve survival prediction in cohorts with few events. An external model may capture useful covariate associations yet systematically overestimate or underestimate risk in the target population, creating a need for selective borrowing. We propose Source Projection Transfer (SPT) for fixed-horizon prediction with a target generalized additive model. SPT requires only source predictions at target covariates, supporting generalized additive, Cox and neural-network source models without individual-level source data. It projects source log-odds scores onto the target basis and borrows through two separately adapted channels: a projection-centered penalty transfers effect shapes, while intercept-recalibrated soft labels inform probabilities at the target risk level. Under local asymptotics, projection avoids the strictly positive risk cost of estimating an uninformative additional source direction. Each channel asymptotically switches off under its corresponding persistent-mismatch condition. In log-logistic and Weibull simulations with covariate shift, SPT improves mean Brier score and discrimination over target-only modeling in all 24 setting-distribution-horizon combinations. Matched comparisons show improvements over borrowing through source probabilities alone across settings, and over borrowing the complete source score under structural mismatch. In UK Biobank-to-SPRINT mortality prediction among standard-treatment participants with reduced kidney function, SPT improves mean discrimination at 24, 30 and 36 months, with Brier improvements at 24 and 36 months. SPT enables flexible source learners to inform a parsimonious target model while adapting to differences between populations.

title: Maxwell-Consistent 3-D Magnetic Field Camera using Scalar-Potential-Based Reconstruction
summary: Various applications require accurate 3-D characterization of magnetic fields with high spatial and temporal resolution. Building on our previously introduced spherical magnetic field camera employing 86 three-axis Hall sensors arranged on a spherical surface, we present a novel magnetic-field reconstruction approach based on the magnetic scalar potential and its spherical harmonic expansion. Unlike the previous reconstruction method that expands each vector component separately, our scalar-potential-based formulation is inherently consistent with Maxwell's equations for source-free fields by design, yielding curl-free and divergence-free field models. Using a simulated magnetic gradient field generated by two permanent magnets, we demonstrate that the proposed method achieves higher reconstruction accuracy, improved robustness to sensor noise and failure, and substantially reduced non-physical divergence and curl compared to the component-wise baseline. Furthermore, the scalar-potential approach attains superior performance with fewer coefficients, indicating a more efficient use of measurement data allowing higher-degree polynomial representations.

title: Unsupervised Feature Selection Using Local Intrinsic Dimensionality -- Extended Version
comment: Preprint submitted to Elsevier Pattern Recognition
summary: High dimensionality degrades both the efficiency and the effectiveness of learning algorithms, and in many applications no class labels are available to guide dimensionality reduction. This paper proposes LIDFS, an unsupervised feature selection method based on Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID). The method builds on the formal equivalence between LID and the indiscriminability of distance measures. The data matrix is transposed so that each feature is treated as a point, and the LID of each feature is estimated by maximum likelihood from the distances to its $k$ nearest neighboring features. Features with lower LID exhibit greater local discriminability and receive higher importance scores. A refinement step then retains one representative per feature neighborhood and demotes locally redundant features. The result is a complete ranking from which any number of features can be selected without rerunning the procedure. LIDFS does not use any information about labels or the number of classes, and runs in $\mathcal{O}(d^2 n)$ time for $n$ instances and $d$ features. LIDFS is compared with classic and state-of-the-art methods and a random baseline on 23 high-dimensional datasets, the classic benchmark collection. The evaluation uses classification accuracy and AUC with five downstream classifiers, as well as clustering accuracy and normalized mutual information, over both full and aggressive selection ranges. LIDFS ranks first in the supervised evaluations and first or tied second in the clustering-based evaluations. It belongs to the top statistical group together with methods that require the number of classes, and it runs faster than its closest competitor. Several recent methods, by contrast, fail to outperform the random baseline. A sensitivity analysis shows that small neighborhood sizes yield the best results.

title: Discrete total variation under the multinomial, Part 3: expectation under a general distribution
summary: For multinomial counts $X\sim\operatorname{Mult}(N;\mathbf p)$ on $n$ ordered bins and a reference law $\mathbf r$ we study the expectation of the reference-centered discrete total variation $d_{\mathbf r}(X)=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}|(X_{j+1}-Nr_{j+1})-(X_j-Nr_j)|$, the natural extension of the comb-test statistic to a non-uniform null. For a non-uniform null the raw total variation of the counts carries a deterministic staircase of order $N$ that no centering of the statistic removes; the counts are therefore centered at the reference law, and under the null ($\mathbf p=\mathbf r$) the statistic is the matched $d_{\mathbf p}$. Exact finite-sample expectations are obtained by conditioning on the total mass in each adjacent pair, which reduces every edge to a translated binomial absolute-deviation problem. For fixed $n\ge3$ and a sampling law bounded away from the boundary of the simplex, the matched statistic admits a three-term asymptotic expansion in powers of $1/N$ whose coefficients are explicit continuous periodic functions of $N(p_{j+1}-p_j)$ (a generalized, non-Poincaré asymptotic expansion), obtained by a weighted local Edgeworth estimate and a corner Euler--Maclaurin summation; all half-integer orders vanish by parity. Each correction separates into a smooth Edgeworth part and an oscillatory lattice part, the latter an Edgeworth perturbation of one formal Euler--Maclaurin series of a Gaussian lattice sum. Under a sampling law $\mathbf p\neq\mathbf r$ the leading expectation is the folded-normal profile implied by the central limit theorem; under local alternatives we identify the $O(1)$ correction (a skewness term, plus a variance-gradient term for Pitman alternatives), and fixed alternatives give a law-of-large-numbers limit, the $\ell_1$ distance between the adjacent-gradient profiles of $\mathbf p$ and $\mathbf r$, on which threshold tests are consistent.

title: Dynamic Persuasion: Managing Reputation under Censored Feedback
comment: 44 pages, 8 figures. A preliminary version of part of this work appears in Proc. IEEE CDC 2026
summary: We study a long-run sender who repeatedly communicates about a state to a sequence of myopic receivers and whose credibility is a public score updated from past interactions. Receivers face a lemon loss and an opportunity loss, and their behavior depends on these only through a single index, the tolerance. Because the score records only detected misrepresentations, it rests above the sender's true honesty rate; we characterize this credibility premium in closed form. In a fluid limit in which the score adjusts slowly, no policy earns more than operating at a single credibility level, and the sender's gain from managing credibility equals the value of the premium: against receivers who correct for imperfect detection, that gain vanishes. At a fixed adjustment speed, every policy is bounded by the fluid value plus a term linear in the speed. We then study three policy classes, linear, (s,S), and threshold, obtain the optimal parameters of the linear and threshold classes in closed form, show how receiver losses shape them, and show that, under an approximation, the optimal (s,S) band collapses to a threshold. Simulations of the dynamics agree with the closed forms and indicate where the single-level conclusion stops: bands pay when switching modes is costly, and cycles pay when demand is seasonal.

title: Apriel Voice 27B Preview: An Open Model for Speech, Reasoning, and Tool Use
summary: A capable voice assistant must do more than recognize words; it must understand requests, reason over context, sustain conversations, and act through tools. We present Apriel Voice 27B Preview, an open speech-language model that unifies these capabilities within a shared reasoning backbone while retaining text and image input modalities. Built on the post-trained Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint, Apriel Voice directly processes speech and generates both responses and tool calls without requiring a separate dialogue model. We introduce a two-stage training procedure to adapt the model to speech. The first stage establishes the speech interface, while the second jointly adapts the projector and backbone through supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and source-dependent cross-entropy and forward Kullback--Leibler divergence supervision. Automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues provide conversational training data, while local teacher serving, overlapping teacher and student computation, and fused full-vocabulary losses enable efficient online distillation. In thinking mode, Apriel Voice achieves a score of 98.90 on Big Bench Audio, 81.13 on Speech-BFCL, and a task success rate of 65.51% on $τ$-Voice, with a mean latency of 1.91 seconds. It also achieves 51.27% English EVA accuracy and 74.13% experience pass@1. Finally, we deploy Apriel Voice 27B Preview on a custom serving platform to support interactive voice interactions.

title: Instrumental Transfer Learning for Solution Operators
summary: Data-driven learning for the solution operator of a differential equation has broad scientific importance, but observations from a target system are often scarce and costly to collect. Related source systems may provide abundant observations under similar physical conditions, whereas even small changes in the governing equation can induce complex changes in the solution operator, making naive data pooling ineffective. We propose a structured transfer learning method that accounts for unknown sparse differences in the governing equations from a known library of candidate terms. Using the resolvent identity and a whitened instrumental variable approach, we construct unbiased source estimating equations for the target operator. Building on these equations, we develop a three-stage estimator that consists of a target-only ridge pilot, source-wise sparse calibration, and a projected refit designed to remove the leading calibration error inherited from the pilot. An iterative recalibration scheme further reduces the remaining error. We establish non-asymptotic prediction bounds showing when transfer achieves the pooled all-source rate, together with minimax lower bounds that characterize both rate optimality and fundamental identifiability limits under common shifts. Simulations and an electronic band-pass filter application demonstrate clear gains over target-only learning, naive pooling and existing transfer methods.

title: Inter-Frame Predictive Contour Coding for Semantic Map Compression
comment: 4 pages, 4 figures, to be presented at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Visual Communications and Image Processing, Singapore, December 2026
summary: Dynamic semantic maps have become an important intermediate representation for many computer vision applications. Efficient lossless compression of such maps is essential for reducing storage and transmission costs.
