Existing contour-based semantic map compression methods mainly exploit spatial redundancy within individual frames while largely ignoring the strong temporal correlation between adjacent semantic maps. In this paper, we propose an inter-frame predictive contour coding framework for lossless semantic map compression. The proposed framework first predicts blob positions and label indexes from the reference frame and then performs contour prediction using corresponding chain-code units in the reference contours. A mode selection mechanism is further employed to choose between intra and inter coding according to the estimated coding cost. By exploiting temporal contour redundancy while preserving the advantages of contour-based representation, the proposed framework significantly improves coding efficiency. Experimental results on the VSPW dynamic semantic segmentation dataset demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art lossless semantic map compression methods. Compared with the recent context-adaptive extended chain coding framework, the proposed inter-frame coding achieves an average bitrate reduction of 3.0\% without significant increase in the average encoding time, demonstrating an effective trade-off between compression performance and computational complexity. The source code is made publicly available at https://github.com/InterDigitalInc/LosslessSegmentationMapCompression.

title: Certified Behavioral Retention for Continual Adaptation with Held-Out Anchors
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Continual Learning in the Era of Foundation Models and Embodied Agents (CL4M / CL4FMAgents)
summary: Continual adaptation requires deciding not only how to update a model, but whether to commit an update without exceeding a declared budget for changes to protected behavior. We introduce Certified Anchor-Based Adaptation (CABA), a candidate-agnostic post-update gate that reserves historical observations from candidate optimization, compares old and candidate policies on frozen representations, and selects the largest tested interpolation coefficient whose worst-anchor forward KL divergence remains within budget. The finite check requires neither action labels nor complete trajectories. We develop a theory-led certification framework that separates measured anchor retention from conditional off-anchor guarantees. Under explicit representation-coverage and Lipschitz assumptions, an accepted update satisfies a uniform behavioral-divergence bound on protected support. The analysis gives regularity bounds for affine softmax heads, probabilistic coverage and compression guarantees, interpolation monotonicity conditions, grid-resolution bounds, and trajectory-level and sequential-composition guarantees. In a controlled UCI Human Activity Recognition study used as a non-stationary sensor-policy proxy, CABA reduces mean forgetting from 1.01 percent for unconstrained adaptation to 0.00 percent at budget epsilon = 0.05, while reducing final average accuracy from 93.04 percent to 88.48 percent. The experiment illustrates a retention-plasticity trade-off and does not establish foundation-model or robotic performance. CABA provides an auditable retention check for candidate generators exposing comparable policy distributions and a declared update path, while deployment also requires separate evidence of current-task utility.

title: Coarse-Graining Optimal Transport for Rollout-Free Post-Training of Flow Matching
summary: Flow matching depends critically on the coupling used to pair source and target samples. Optimal transport (OT) couplings can reduce velocity conflict and straighten trajectories; but, in practice, challenges remain: the source comes from a continuous distribution, only a finite number of target samples data are accessible, and the neural network has finite capacity. For these reasons, making the coupling more OT-like may not consistently improve sampling quality, in particular in the low number-of-function-evaluation (NFE) regime. Motivated by this, we introduce ReCouple, a controllable framework that constructs coarse-grained OT couplings, to better understand rollout-free OT-based post-training. We also consider extensions of this basic framework: ReCouple+ extends this toward the continuous-source setting by increasing source resolution, converging to semi-discrete OT in the appropriate limit; and ReCouple++ further adds spatial regularization, motivated by the observation that straight trajectories need not correspond to spatially simple velocity fields. Empirical validation demonstrates the effectiveness of these methods, and it reveals an NFE-dependent interplay between coupling optimality, neural realizability, and generation quality.

title: Approximate Dynamic Programming for Link Reconfiguration to Reduce Malicious Input Controllability in Consensus Networks
summary: Communication links influence how strongly a malicious input at one sensor affects a consensus network. We study how a defender can reduce this influence by selecting one additional link after observing the currently attacked sensor. The attacked sensor changes over time, and vulnerability is measured by the trace of a finite-horizon controllability Gramian. A prescribed local epsilon-greedy attacker response rule defines a discounted Markov decision process for the defender. Exact dynamic programming (DP) provides an optimal policy using the full Gramian payoff matrix and attacker transition model. We then introduce approximate dynamic programming (ADP) that learns from sampled attacker transitions and empirical Gramian costs estimated from measured impulse responses. Under conditionally unbiased costs and standard sampling and learning-rate conditions, the learned action-value table converges to the exact DP solution. The analysis uses Bellman contraction and bounds the effect of persistent Gramian estimation bias, establishing when measured responses recover optimal defender decisions without constructing the full payoff matrix. In simulations on 20- and 100-node graphs, empirical ADP rollout costs are within 0.23% and 1.76%, respectively, of exact DP. In a two-dimensional intruder tracking example, both policies reduce network-wide root-mean-square tracking error spread by approximately 25% relative to an unmitigated attack.

title: Prevented is Not Protected: What Attack Success Rate Hides about RAG
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is vulnerable to knowledge poisoning, where adversaries manipulate retrieved evidence to influence model outputs. Existing defenses are primarily evaluated using attack success rate (ASR), which obscures defense-induced failures and the mechanisms behind apparent attack prevention. To address this issue, this work introduces \textbf{Aligned RAG Evaluation}, a matched-query protocol that jointly examines clean and poisoned responses, with and without defense. By combining matched conditions analysis, LLM-judge endorsement, and retrieval dependence controls, the proposed framework distinguishes prevented from introduced failures, target mentions from LLM endorsement, and single-passage influence from evidence composition. Experiments on HotpotQA and Natural Questions reveal that existing defenses can introduce unexpected target-positive answers, although they can prevent some attacks, while evaluation criteria can also change defense rankings. Our findings expose critical blind spots in ASR-based evaluation and motivate a more comprehensive assessment of RAG poisoning defenses. The code and the evaluation artifact are available at https://github.com/chxhana/aligned-rag-eval.

title: Dimension Changes the Scale-Signal Channel in Nearest-Neighbor Two-Sample Testing
summary: Nearest-neighbor two-sample tests are often analyzed with dimension fixed. We study the power of the generalized edge-count test on a directed 1-nearest-neighbor graph. This statistic combines a weighted sum and a difference of the two within-sample edge counts. For balanced isotropic Gaussian samples with $d/\log N\toγ>0$, we derive the connection probabilities under local location and scale alternatives. Under location alternatives, the two counts have equal mean shifts, which cancel in their difference. Under scale alternatives, the two counts instead have mean shifts of opposite signs. We also derive the growth rate of the null expectation $\mathbb{E}_0C_3$, where $C_3$ counts pairs of directed edges sharing exactly one vertex. On an explicit range of $γ$, we establish local-power limits strictly above the test level for scale alternatives in the difference component at the scale $|\varepsilon_N|\asymp (\mathbb{E}_0C_3)^{1/2}/(Nd)$. Here $\mathbb{E}_0C_3$ gives the variance order of the difference count under these local alternatives. At this scale, the standardized drift of the weighted sum vanishes. When $d=1$, the weighted component instead detects local Gaussian scale alternatives while the difference component has no limiting drift. Thus dimension changes both the magnitude of a detectable scale difference and the component of the test that detects it.

title: A Mixed $H_{\infty}$--Passivity Approach for Leveraging Heat-Pump-Connected District Heating Systems as Frequency Support in Electric Power Systems
summary: Heat-pump (HP)-connected district heating systems (DHSs) can support grid frequency by rapidly modulating HP electrical consumption while accommodating the resulting heat imbalance. Thermal-state-informed HP control improves EPS--DHS coordination, but introduces slower DHS dynamics and heat-side disturbance propagation at the electrical interface on the time scale of secondary frequency control. This paper formulates the regulated DHS as a grid-facing dynamic port and develops a mixed $H_\infty$--passivity framework for disturbance-independent temperature regulation while preserving a clean electrical response during secondary frequency control. Sufficient conditions guarantee local asymptotic stability of the EPS--HP--DHS interconnection across primary frequency control, secondary frequency control, and DHS regulation. These stability conditions are integrated with multi-channel $H_\infty$ attenuation of DHS-state-dependent electrical dynamics, heat-disturbance propagation, and DHS-regulation errors, yielding a tractable convex LMI program for controller synthesis. Cross-model validation deploys controllers synthesized on control-oriented EPS--DHS models, without retuning, on an open-source electromechanical IEEE 39-bus model coupled with four high-fidelity finite-volume DHS models retaining thermal transport, storage, and heat-loss dynamics. The resulting controller improves EPS--DHS coordination without compromising the grid-facing electrical response.

title: CLIC: Closed-Loop Intent Consistency for Securing LLM-Driven Control in Open RAN
summary: With the progressive capabilities of large language models (LLMs), researchers are finding ways to integrate them into the control loops of Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) to enable slicing and resource management through user intents. However, integration of LLMs in the O-RAN control loop via the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) makes the system vulnerable to \textit{runtime prompt injection threats}, which manipulate control decisions without violating interface authentication, and \textit{residual virtual prompt injection (VPI)} attacks that plant trigger mechanisms to silently steer the behaviour during fine-tuning. Existing studies address only the runtime threat and do not enforce consistency across the full control path, i.e. from the certified A1 intent, through the multi-step LLM trajectory, to the final E2 action. We propose a closed-loop intent-consistency layer (CLIC) that jointly mitigates both threats. The proposed CLIC defines a formal consistency score using a small quantized language model, which is deployed as a Non-RT rApp for model-integrity certification along with a Near-RT xApp for runtime enforcement. We implement CLIC on the OpenAI Cellular (OAIC) platform and evaluate it under domain-adapted JailbreakBench, AdvBench, and VPI workloads. The experimental results show that the proposed CLIC reduces the attack success rate from 0.92 to 0.29 and residual VPI attacks from 0.37 to 0.04, while improving isolation and fairness at slightly higher latency costs, i.e. approximately 27 ms.

title: Truthful and Admissible Principal--Agent Testing with Nuisance Parameters
summary: Statistical contracts reward experimenters according to the evidence produced by a costly study, so the reward rule influences both who participates and what they report. Principal--agent testing theory explains how to prevent ineffective proposals from being profitable. We ask when such contracts can also elicit honest parameter reports if the decision concerns a mean effect but the variance or distributional shape is unknown. Under risk neutrality and a fixed participation cost, we construct menus of e-values --- nonnegative normalized rewards with expected value at most one under every null --- such that (i) agents who know they are null have no incentive to participate, (ii) every alternative type earns positive expected profit and is thus incentivized to participate, (iii) truthful reporting uniquely maximizes expected their reward, (iv) and each contract is admissible: its payouts cannot be pointwise improved while retaining null validity. For Gaussian observations, we treat separately agents who know both mean and variance and agents who know only their mean; in the latter case, truthfulness holds at every variance without requiring a nuisance prior. Multi-sample extensions preserve these incentives and can reward accumulating evidence. Beyond Gaussian models, we show that two independent nonnegative observations suffice to elicit any finite mean above a positive null threshold, without any further distributional knowledge, but one observation cannot combine strict mean elicitation with individual admissibility on this class. Finally, we distinguish the existence of useful tests from the identification needed for truthful contracts. Boundedness is not required, and finitely many null constraints do not by themselves guarantee admissible elicitation.

title: Learning the Omega-Limit Partition from Approximate Koopman Invariants
summary: Nonlinear dynamical systems with multiple omega-limit sets pose a fundamental challenge for global finite-dimensional Koopman modeling with continuous observables. A natural way to address this challenge is to decompose the state space into forward-invariant regions associated with distinct asymptotic behaviors and to learn a separate Koopman model for each region. This paper studies how to compute such partitions from data. We establish conditions under which Koopman-invariant observables, namely eigenfunctions associated with the unit eigenvalue, characterize the stationary partition induced by omega-limit sets. Building on this characterization, we develop OPAL (Omega-limit Partitions from Approximate invariants Learned from data), an algorithm that extracts partitions from approximate invariant observables. Numerical examples show that the recovered partitions capture the relevant asymptotic regions and support multiple regional linear Koopman models with significantly improved long-horizon prediction capabilities.

title: What It Costs to Trust a Source: A Reproducible Method for Institutional Assessment of Author Disambiguation
summary: Records of research outputs are curated with care by universities, and the effort is shaped by the external sources from which candidate records are drawn. The curation required before the author identities in such sources can be trusted is examined, and a reproducible method for estimating its cost is set out. Four tests are described; two can be run on public data alone, and two are conducted against an institution's own curated record, taken from Symplectic Elements Discovery portals. The method is demonstrated on OpenAlex and Dimensions across 30 institutions. Of the publications attributed to matched researchers, 50.4\% were confirmed by the institutional record for OpenAlex and 69.6\% for Dimensions, and fewer trusted researcher profiles were retained from OpenAlex at a matched confidence threshold in each of the 30 institutions. Carried through to effort, integrating OpenAlex requires 1.5 times the person-days of review and entry of Dimensions even when each feed is filtered at the threshold that minimises the amount of review required.

title: Conditional Neural SDEs for Financial Time-Series Generation
summary: Conditional generation of time-series paths is a central problem in probabilistic modeling, where the goal is to simulate future trajectories that are both realistic and responsive to external context. It has direct applications in finance and economics. Neural stochastic differential equations provide a natural framework for this task by combining continuous-time stochastic dynamics with learnable drift and diffusion functions. However, directly modeling the target state can be unstable in conditional settings, especially when the target and conditioning variables have strong level dependence, limited training data, or different dimensions.We propose a residualanchor Neural SDE architecture that decomposes the target into a learned conditional anchor and a stochastic residual. The anchor captures the context-dependent baseline, while the Neural SDE (Stochastic Differential Equation) models the residual dynamics around this baseline. This separation reduces the burden on the stochastic dynamics and generalizes spread-based representations to more general conditioning settings.We evaluate the approach on real-world financial time series, including conditional interest-rate scenarios and a comparison with a time-series foundation model. The results show that the proposed model can generate plausible conditional paths, maintain competitive point accuracy, and provide calibrated uncertainty estimates.

title: A Temporal Cellular Sheaf Framework for Multi-Agent Systems with Switching Communication Topologies
summary: Cellular sheaves serve as a natural modeling framework for encoding heterogeneity in the state and interaction spaces of multi-agent systems. This work examines switching communication graphs with the use of temporal cellular sheaves, which we construct to represent heterogeneous agent state spaces, the maps that relate them, and their respective communication constraints. We then develop sufficient conditions under which a multi-agent system defined on a temporal cellular sheaf can solve the target tracking problem by generalizing the existing concept of joint connectivity. Using a Lyapunov-based stability analysis, we demonstrate that the target tracking error of the network converges to a neighborhood of the origin.

title: Mage-VL-Cowork: A Full Training Recipe to Learn Hybrid Computer Use From Evolved Harnesses
summary: Effective computer-use agents (CUAs) should seamlessly combine visual GUI interaction with code and terminal execution within a single policy. We present Mage-VL-Cowork, a 4B hybrid CUA trained from a general multimodally aligned checkpoint through an end-to-end, progressive five-stage curriculum across midtraining, SFT, and RL. To power this curriculum at scale, Mage-CUA-Forge replaces per-task agent construction with reusable, skill-conditioned generation workflows and application-specific preparers, synthesizing 293,806 desktop and web tasks across 6,915 skills while reducing recurring per-task expenditure by 82.6%. Rather than directly distilling a default teacher, we evolve the teacher harness and instantiate specialized CUA harnesses to yield high-quality trajectories alongside stage-specific supervision. Mage-VL-Cowork-4B finally climbs to 66.0% on OSWorld-Verified through different training stages with more efficient reasoning cost, achieving state-of-the-art performance at its parameter size and pushing forward the frontier of on-device intelligence.

title: Simultaneous inference for additive regression
summary: This paper develops methods for simultaneous inference on component functions in additive models. We first propose bias-corrected smooth backfitting estimators inspired by least squares linear regression and establish their asymptotic properties. We then show that the distributions of the uniform errors of these estimators converge to a Gumbel-type distribution. Based on this distributional approximation, we construct simultaneous confidence bands and develop a practical residual-based procedure for testing the additive components. Simulation studies and empirical data analyses demonstrate that the proposed estimators reduce bias and improve estimation accuracy compared with several existing estimators. Moreover, the empirical coverage probabilities of the proposed simultaneous confidence bands are found to be comparable to those of their oracle counterparts.

title: Automated Optimization of Patient-Specific Electro-Anatomical Models Fitted to Cochlear Implant SCINSEV
summary: Purpose: Patient-specific electro-anatomical models (EAMs) of the implanted cochlea are crucial for auditory nerve fiber simulation in cochlear implant (CI) programming and neural health estimation. Fitting an EAM to the stimulation current induced non-stimulating electrode voltage (SCINSEV) currently requires manual expert adjustment or exhaustive search over precomputed forward solutions, neither of which scales to routine clinical use. We present an automated optimization pipeline that fits patient specific EAMs in minutes. Methods: Four compartment tissue label maps (perilymph, soft tissue, modiolus, and bone) derived from postoperative CT were used to construct a finite difference forward model, fitted to the measured SCINSEV by Gaussian process Bayesian optimization. Three reductions cut fitting cost: a coarsened grid with trilinear injection and readout at sub-voxel contact positions; solving half the stimulating contacts and completing three quarters of the matrix by reciprocity; and a Jacobian-based identifiability analysis reducing four resistivities to two. Each reduction was validated separately against the measurement's reciprocity residual and the reproducibility of the fit. Results: Across 43 implanted ears, fitting took a median of 2.6 minutes per ear. Median SCINSEV RMSE on the reduced-resolution objective was 0.069 mV, against 0.084 mV for grid search at a matched evaluation budget. Against an exhaustive full-resolution grid search requiring a median of 9.1 hours per ear, the pipeline reached statistically indistinguishable fitting error roughly 210x faster. Conclusion: Patient-specific cochlear EAM fitting can be performed at clinically practical timescales without expert supervision, removing a major computational barrier to patient-specific cochlear implant programming and cochlear simulation.

title: WorldBridge: Bridging Video and Action for Task Generalization in World Action Models
comment: Authors are listed in alphabetical order. Project page: https://worldbridge-jd.github.io/
summary: Achieving the broad task generalization of embodied models in physical environments remains a central challenge in robot learning. We study this challenge in World Action Models (WAMs) through two complementary capabilities: video generalization, which predicts the visual evolution of new tasks, and action generalization, which translates these predictions into executable behavior through a video-to-action bridge. By varying video and action supervision for tasks outside an initial training set, we examine their respective contributions to task transfer. On RoboTwin 2.0, using only in-distribution video-action supervision yields a 25.07% success rate on out-of-distribution tasks. Introducing videos of these tasks without their action labels raises success to 55.90%, while adding just one action-labeled demonstration per task further improves it to 70.70%. These findings suggest that broader video coverage enables task transfer by leveraging existing inverse-dynamics capabilities, while even sparse action supervision further strengthens those capabilities. Guided by this perspective, we introduce WorldBridge, a WAM with separate video and action experts connected through structured attention and trained with joint flow matching. WorldBridge incorporates visual memory at two temporal scales and action forcing, alongside a unified data processing pipeline that standardizes and filters heterogeneous robot trajectories and egocentric hand-derived supervision. Across multiple manipulation benchmarks, WorldBridge achieves state-of-the-art performance among the compared methods, including 96.23% on RoboTwin 2.0 full data setting and 80.9% on clean to random setting, 82.8% on RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, and 57.6% on DOMINO Level-1. Our study highlights the complementary roles of video prediction and action grounding in developing robots that generalize across tasks.

title: Advancing Specific Local Wine Identification through Integration of ICP-MS Mineral Wine Profiles and Machine Learning: A Case Study on Discrimination Among the Ten Beaujolais Crus
summary: The Beaujolais vineyard, located in France's Auvergne-Rh{ô}ne-Alpes region, is internationally recognized for its geological diversity and the strong identity of its ten crus. Guaranteeing authenticity of these appellations is essential for producers and regulators, as mislabeling and fraud can undermine both economic value and consumer trust. In this study, we introduce the Mineral Wine Profile (MWP), a high-throughput ICP-MS protocol enabling the semi-quantitative analysis of more than 40 mineral elements. A total of 1288 Gamay wines from the 2022 and 2023 vintages, collected across the ten Beaujolais crus, were analyzed. Multivariate statistical methods and machine learning were applied to assess their discriminatory power. Principal Component Analysis clearly separated vintages, while Random Forest models achieved 98% accuracy for vintage classification. Mixture Discriminant Analysis further differentiated the ten crus with an average accuracy of 92%. Misclassifications mostly occurred between geographically neighboring crus, reflecting overlapping soil structures and terroir continuity. Element-soil correlations (e.g., Fe enriched in clay-rich soils, Mn in sandy soils, Cs in silty soils) provided mechanistic insights into terroir differentiation. These results confirm that wine mineral fingerprints can act as reliable chemical memories of origin. By combining elemental profiling with Machine Learning, this work demonstrates a robust, reproducible, and scalable approach for intra-regional wine authentication. Beyond its scientific contribution, the MWP approach offers practical applications for the valorization of terroirs, protection of Appellations d'Origine Contr{ô}l{é}e (AOC), and fraud prevention in the wine industry.

title: Optimal climate policy in incomplete electricity markets
summary: Incomplete long-term contracting in electricity markets can expose investors and consumers to inefficient levels of risk. This paper investigates how incompleteness impacts the optimal choice of climate policy. We develop a game-theoretic model of optimal policy-making in anticipation of how electricity market agents react to a given policy when gas prices and demand are uncertain and contracting is incomplete. In illustrative experiments, we observe that renewable subsidies and carbon prices induce an insurance co-benefit when markets are incomplete. This is because, relative to a complete market benchmark, incompleteness shifts investment from renewables toward gas and exposes consumers to uninsured risk from inter-annual volatility in electricity prices. By incentivizing investment in renewables, subsidies and carbon prices indirectly counteract these distortions. Consequently, incompleteness increases the optimal subsidy and carbon price levels in our experiments. Renewable subsidies exhibit a stronger insurance effect than carbon pricing, as the latter leads to more investment in gas with carbon capture and storage and more volatile electricity prices. While carbon pricing is more economically efficient than subsidies in complete markets, incompleteness shrinks its efficiency advantage and even leads to cases where subsidies are more economically efficient.

title: Safin-1.5: Safety-Native Architecture and Verifiable Reasoning for Recursive Safety Improvement
summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) enables large language models to advance their capabilities through successive updates, but these updates can also introduce new risks and weaken existing safeguards. In line with the AI-45° Law, we pursue Safety RSI, in which safety develops as an intrinsic capability alongside general model capabilities through continual risk discovery and repair, while preserving utility and limiting over-refusal. We introduce Safin-1.5, a model built on a safety architecture and trained through recursive safety improvement, with an inference-time harness that extends its capabilities to formal reasoning. Our approach comprises three components: i) The safety architecture combines persistent safety states with hazardous-knowledge disentanglement. The former retains and selectively invokes safety knowledge, while the latter relocates targeted hazardous knowledge into removable experts, enabling its removal with minimal impact on general capabilities. ii) Recursive safety improvement establishes a discovery-evaluation-repair loop. The loop identifies new vulnerabilities and uses experimental feedback to develop repair strategies. It accepts updates only when they improve safety while preserving general capabilities and limiting over-refusal. iii) The formal reasoning harness combines the model's language understanding with symbolic inference and verification. Proof-obligation-guided semantic bridging recovers missing relations in formal representations, enabling symbolic solvers to construct checkable proofs under formalized premises and accepted semantic bridges. Experimental results demonstrate that Safin-1.5 achieves safety and reasoning performance, outperforming frontier models.

title: Reliability-Weighted Direct Preference Optimization: Penalized Weights for Robust Preference Learning
summary:
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) treats every reported comparison as correct, yet preference data contain
  reversed, tied or otherwise noisy comparisons. RW-DPO gives each comparison an unknown reliability weight
  $w_i\in[0,1]$ that enters the likelihood linearly -- DPO is $w\equiv1$, a reversed comparison $w_i=0$ -- and estimates
  the weights jointly with the policy under a minimax-concave penalty on $-\log w_i$. The penalty keeps every
  comparison the model agrees with at exactly $w_i=1$ and acts only on those it contradicts, through closed-form weight
  updates at negligible cost over DPO. We prove that recovering all flipped comparisons from a single annotation per
  comparison requires margins of order $\log n$. Furthermore, in a linear-index model, starting from an initial fit
  pointing in the correct direction, our estimator jointly consistently recovers the preference direction and weights,
  as well as identifies the flipped comparisons above this margin scale, even when a fixed fraction of comparisons is
  flipped. In simulations RW-DPO has the lowest average estimation error among DPO, noise-rate corrections and recent
  robust methods, with far more precise flags than recent label-correction methods. In DPO fine-tuning of a language
  model with 10-30% flipped labels, its win rate does not fall as the flip rate grows and exceeds that of DPO trained on
  clean labels, matching the strongest recent method with corrections concentrated on the flipped labels.

title: Prediction-Induced Sparsity for Tracked FMCW Radar: A Track-Conditioned Event-Gap FPGA Architecture
summary: Tracked FMCW radar already carries a prediction of the next target state, yet the downstream digital hardware is commonly provisioned for a fixed spectral search. We present prediction-induced sparsity (PIS), a tracked-mode architecture that uses the prior before event formation and hardware scheduling. The predicted beat is derotated to an innovation-centred coordinate, while tracker covariance is propagated to a bounded residual support K. Sparse level-crossing packets are then executed by an exact event-gap resonator engine with a shared complex processing element and K-dependent state/coefficient memory. On a public FMCW dataset, causal prior-only con- ditioning reduces event records by 33.1% on average, and the representative fixed-point stream is bit-exact in RTL. And on an Artix-7 implementation, reducing physical support from 129 to 23 states lowers LUT and BRAM use by 65.0% and 88.1%, respectively, and reduces measured VCCINT power by 19.9% at matched throughput. The results show how tracking uncertainty can become a hardware-capacity implication for future adaptive radar accelerators.

title: PathoJev: Efficient Pathology Decisions from Shared Visual Context
summary: Pathology workflows require multiple visual judgments about the same slide, from identifying tumor type to assessing grade and invasion. Generating and parsing a separate textual response for each structured question adds latency between visual evidence and usable decisions. Building on the System One paradigm, we introduce PathoJev, a pathology model that directly predicts answer probabilities for whole-slide and region-level assessment. PathoJev encodes each slide once and evaluates independent question suffixes in batches over the shared visual context. Reusing the hybrid backbone's recurrent states further limits the computation that grows with slide-context length for each additional question. Across three whole-slide benchmarks, the 9B and 27B models achieve mean accuracies of 77.2% and 78.1%, exceeding SlideChat by 5.4 and 6.3 percentage points. Both scales also maintain competitive accuracy on five ROI benchmarks. On WSI-Bench, the 9B model runs 9.1x faster than SlideChat. Shared context accelerates eight-question workloads by 6.9x and 5.9x over separate prefix encoding, rising to 11.2x and 8.9x for 64 questions. These results provide a reusable probabilistic interface for combining multiple visual judgments in whole-slide and local tissue assessment. Code: https://github.com/ChyaZhang/PathoJev.

title: PDE-Residual-Informed Kriging
summary: Physics-informed Gaussian process (GP) methods provide a probabilistic framework for PDE solving. Existing approaches incorporate PDE information in different ways: pointwise conditioning uses the governing equation only at finitely many selected locations, globally constrained GPs restrict the admissible functions to satisfy the PDE exactly, and residual-penalized methods control the PDE mismatch over the whole domain through an additional penalty weight. What is still missing is a GP formulation that directly incorporates global PDE-residual information of the entire domain into its covariance structure, while retaining model flexibility and standard GP conditioning without a separate residual-weight parameter. To solve this issue, this study proposes PDE-residual-informed Kriging (PRIK) based on a PDE-residual kernel. The PDE-residual kernel is constructed by equipping a kernel-section space with an inner product defined by the $L^{2}$ inner product of PDE residuals. This construction makes PRIK yield the posterior mean with minimum integrated squared PDE residual. It also provides direct statistical interpretations: the variance-scale estimate equals the normalized PDE-residual energy (i.e., the integrated squared PDE residual of the posterior mean divided by the number of labeled observations), and the profile likelihood balances this residual energy against model complexity. Under the stated regularity and stability conditions, we establish $H^{2}$-quasi-optimality and convergence rates for the posterior mean, together with a nonasymptotic bound for its PDE-residual norm. We further show that the normalized posterior kernel converges to a variational Green-type kernel and derive a uniform nonasymptotic contraction bound for the posterior variance. Numerical studies provide empirical evidence consistent with the theory and demonstrate the PDE-solving capability of PRIK.

title: Market Efficiency and Capacity Investment under Flexible Price-Making Loads: A Computational Study
summary: Large flexible loads such as data centers can shift consumption across locations and hours to lower their bills. We model a price-making consumer leading the system operator in a Stackelberg game and compare its shifts with a cost-minimizing planner's over a simulated RTS-GMLC year. Strategic temporal and spatial shifting capture 75% and 93% of the planner's savings, forgoing the rest mostly by withholding flexibility to protect favorable prices. Scarce capacity and abundant renewables raise this share for temporal shifting; scarce transmission lowers it for spatial shifting. Temporal and spatial flexibility substitute for thermal and transmission capacity, respectively, and complement renewables.

title: "Shall We Approve?" Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents increasingly rely on automated approvers to decide whether a proposed shell command may run. Existing approvers, from rule-based checkers to guardrail models and deployed permission classifiers, base their decisions on the text of the request and command. Yet a command's behavior depends on the code it invokes and the state of the workspace, and systems that observe file changes leave the assessment to the agent or a human after execution. We present Caper, a consequence-aware approval mechanism that pre-executes each command in a snapshotted sandbox, provides an independent approver with a bounded report of its observed effects, commits allowed commands, and rolls back blocked ones with a reason the agent can act on. Compared with six existing systems, Caper achieves the lowest harmful-outcome rate on SABER (6.7% versus at least 14.8%) and YoloFS-Ext, a benchmark we build in which harmful behavior is hidden inside invoked tools (7.8% versus at least 35.3%), while blocking 1.0% of the safe twins of the dangerous tasks in YoloFS-Ext.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for Topological Treatment Effects
summary: We present a unified framework for uncertainty quantification over filtration scale, extending the topological average treatment effect (TATE) analysis of \citet{kim-lee} to conditional mean confidence and individual effect prediction. For the conditional topological average treatment effect (CTATE), we derive multiplier confidence bands at a fixed covariate value, simultaneous over filtration scale, and prove validity in a correctly specified finite-dimensional regression regime, with explicit control of smoothing bias and nuisance-estimation error. For the individual topological treatment effect (ITTE), we integrate existing weighted and functional split-conformal methods to obtain finite-sample marginal prediction coverage under known target-to-calibration likelihood ratios, with a total-variation bound for estimated ratios. We also extend the current TATE silhouette stability analysis to the diagram-independent bound $\|Φ_r(D)-Φ_r(D')\|_\infty \le (1+2r)W_1(D,D')$ for $r\geq1$, recovering the known $r=1$ constant, and propagate diagram approximation error to prediction bands. The installable Python library \texttt{tcda\_uq} integrates mean confidence, individual prediction, and topological preprocessing, with tutorials and reproduction materials. Simulations and a PACCE lesion-measurement application illustrate the distinct coverage targets and the importance of declaring the target population.

title: EMT Assessment of SCR and X/R Effects on Current-Priority-Dependent LVRT Response of a Grid-Following BESS
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE Texas Power and Energy Conference (TPEC 2027)
summary: Low-voltage ride-through (LVRT) forces a grid-following inverter to allocate finite converter current between active- and reactive-current objectives. This paper uses a PSCAD electromagnetic-transient (EMT) representation of an aggregated battery energy storage system (BESS) to quantify how short-circuit ratio (SCR) and grid impedance X/R ratio alter that tradeoff. Active-current priority and reactive-current priority are compared for five paired grid conditions under the same 150-ms balanced three-phase fault, with pre-fault active power approximately 0.84 pu, POI reactive-power exchange near 0 pu, and a 1.0-pu dq-current limit. Fundamental positive-sequence voltage and power are reconstructed from 100-$μ$s three-phase EMT outputs. Across the fixed-fault SCR sweep, the Q-priority late-fault voltage advantage increases from 0.046 pu in the strongest tested grid to 0.129 pu in the weakest; the weakest P-priority case also shows active-power reversal and a pronounced controller-frequency excursion. At fixed SCR, changing X/R produces a smaller increase from 0.092 to 0.112 pu, mainly through reduced P-priority voltage support. Because the common physical fault also deepens the passive retained-voltage condition as SCR decreases, the SCR result is interpreted as a fixed-fault grid-strength sensitivity rather than a constant-sag comparison. Grid strength is the larger sensitivity in the tested matrix, while X/R remains an additional modifier under the studied fault conditions.

title: DyCraft: An Agentic System for Long-Horizon 4D Scene Generation
summary: While frontier coding agents can generate high-quality 3D scenes and articulated assets, they struggle to create coherent long-horizon animations. When equipped with general-purpose harnesses, they frequently produce physically implausible outputs, generating objects that interpenetrate, lack physical support, or move unnaturally. Such bare agents struggle to repair these errors because they default to scripting the full animation in one pass, making it difficult to verify their work and disentangle complex spatiotemporal constraints. Drawing on the practice of human animators, we introduce DyCraft, a system for animated 3D scene generation that breaks animation into steps that coding agents can more reliably solve. DyCraft first expands the user's prompt into a detailed plan and builds a static scene. It then creates a 3D storyboard of key animation poses, where each frame is a static 3D scene that the agent can build and debug in isolation. Storyboarding decomposes the problem into pairs of verified start and end states, allowing the agent to author local motion between them with a collection of motion authoring tools. We evaluate DyCraft on 24 long-horizon, multi-shot animation tasks covering humanoid robots, human and animal characters, and physical mechanisms. Compared with a native GPT-6 agent in Codex and prior agentic baselines, DyCraft substantially reduces physical violations and generates higher-quality animated 3D scenes that are more often preferred by human raters.

title: Stable and efficient covariance estimation for sample L-moments using Hájek projections
summary: L-moments are useful summary statistics and are widely used in statistical analysis. The joint covariance matrix of sample L-moments not only describes their sampling uncertainty but is also needed for covariance-weighted distances and related statistical procedures. An exact unbiased covariance estimator is already available. However, in our previous applications, this estimator sometimes produced singular or indefinite covariance matrices. Such matrices cause problems when matrix inversion is required. The present paper addresses this difficulty. We examine standard positive-definite corrections and two covariance estimators based on leave-one-out sample L-moments: the delete-one jackknife estimator and an estimator based on the Hájek projection. Both are positive semidefinite by construction. Simulation results show that the projection estimator generally has smaller estimation error and better numerical stability than the exact unbiased estimator. The jackknife estimator overestimates the variances of higher-order sample L-moments and has larger estimation error than the projection estimator. We also develop fast rank-prefix algorithms for the three covariance estimators considered. These algorithms substantially reduce computation time.

title: Control-Layer Interpretation of Reactive Power Recovery Limits in EMT-RMS Model Benchmarking of Inverter-Based Resources
comment: Accepted for presentation at IEEE PES Grid Edge Technologies 2027, April 19-22, 2027, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA.5 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables
summary: EMT--RMS benchmarking is widely used to verify cross-platform consistency of inverter-based resource (IBR) dynamic models. This paper examines a 200 MW anonymized IBR represented in PSCAD and PSS/E. The EMT model separates inverter electrical capability from a plant-level power plant controller (PPC) recovery target, whereas the RMS model represents these functions through REECC and REPCA parameters. Directly assigning the PPC target of $\pm 0.2764$ pu to REPCA hard reactive limits is initialization-inconsistent at the original lagging operating point because the initial reactive command is 0.396273 pu. A second, near-unity-power-factor operating point initializes successfully with the same diagnostic limit, demonstrating that the conflict is operating-point dependent. Using the non-conflicting capability mapping removes the original hard-limit conflict, but the benchmark still shows 18.5--30.2 MVAr post-event POI reactive-power differences from PSCAD. A one-at-a-time REPCA $K_c$ sensitivity under matched benchmark initial conditions further shows that RMS recovery is parameter- and limit-dependent: at $K_c=0.05$ and 0.10 the aggregate machine reactive output reaches the configured capability bounds, while $K_c=0.15$ moves VDOWN, VUP, and HVRT off those bounds and changes their settled POI reactive power by 8.94, 18.00, and 3.17 MVAr, respectively. Machine-to-POI accounting further shows why machine-side saturation need not reproduce the POI-level PPC recovery magnitude. The results distinguish initialization feasibility from recovery equivalence and provide a control-layer diagnostic workflow beyond waveform comparison.

title: AutoHebb: Self-Modifying Neural Networks that Zero-Shot Infer and Continually Learn
summary: Humans and animals have a unique capacity to generalize and learn in novel circumstances, including "0-shot" inference (ZI) and continual learning (CL) -- two powerful cognitive abilities. Despite this importance, efforts to model ZI and CL are seriously limited in several ways. First, existing models typically lack components critical to ZI and CL in the brain, namely, strong inductive biases (for ZI) and autonomous control of learning (for CL). Second, models can be less tractable to analysis if model components are overly complex (lacking simplicity), or too task-restricted if model components are overly bespoke (lacking expressivity). Here we introduce autonomous Hebbian networks ("AutoHebb"), a class of online learning feedforward neural networks that realize strong inductive biases and autonomously controlled learning, and are both simple and expressive. Unlike standard models that learn via externally controlled optimization (e.g. gradient descent), AutoHebb networks combine external feedback with internally generated activity to produce a global learning signal ('neuromodulator') fed back to the network. The neuromodulator in turn gates a biologically grounded local learning rule (3-factor Hebbian rule) that updates networks' plastic weights. Using meta-learning to search for fixed (non-plastic) weights, we find that AutoHebb networks (1) succeed on ZI tasks, (2) show emergent (untrained) ZI/CL abilities, (3) admit reverse-engineering into explicit algorithms, and (4) outperform modern learning models on ZI/CL tasks. Lastly, performance comparisons to related models implied an essential role for three model components: meta-learning, Hebbian plasticity, and autonomous control of learning. These findings indicate that AutoHebb may be useful in hypothesis generation, analysis, and discovery of biologically grounded forms of learning and generalization.

title: Unidentified prediction-risk rankings under spatial sampling with fixed inclusion probabilities
comment: 8 pages, including supplementary material; ancillary verification code included
summary: For Gaussian spatial prediction, we construct positive sampling mechanisms with identical observation laws and conditional site inclusion probabilities, yet opposite risk rankings for two fixed predictors. The construction selects two of four sites and allows independent Gaussian measurement error.

title: Delta-Seeker: Closed-Loop Generative Search for Novel Circuit Design Discovery
summary: Generative models are increasingly used for circuit synthesis and optimization by proposing topologies, sizing devices, and exploring large design spaces. We investigate whether they can instead support design discovery, where generated structures must depart from known designs while producing reproducible electrical behavior. We propose Delta-Seeker, a closed-loop circuit search framework that combines discrete diffusion for topology generation and mutation with structural checking, SPICE-in-the-loop sizing, Pareto selection, and feedback from prior search outcomes. The search controller uses progress and recurring structural failures to allocate evaluation effort and steer subsequent topology generation, while independent re-sizing and operating-corner analysis are performed only after search. In generator-only experiments, cross-generation feedback increases structurally valid children from 143 to 945 and reduces the faulty-candidate fraction from 0.925 to 0.761. In op-amp topology discovery at matched sizing cost, Delta-Seeker yields 54 designs that remain feasible in at least three of four independent re-sizings and 18 that additionally pass device-level checks and supply-temperature corner analysis, compared with 38 and 10 under fixed control. Removing cross-generation memory reduces independently robust discoveries from 54 to 43 and seven-corner robust discoveries from 40 to 27. In DC-DC converter search, nearest-parent analysis identifies a corpus-absent topology whose generated switching current path changes its nearest training-corpus parent from infeasible at all four operating corners to feasible at all four, while increasing median efficiency from 31.2% to 98.96%. These results show that closed-loop generative search can support circuit discovery beyond structural novelty by identifying new topologies with independently verified changes in circuit operation.

title: More Rules, Longer Lists? Benchmarking Self-Evolving Agents on a Hidden-Rule Curriculum
summary: Self-evolving agents rewrite a persistent state from feedback, but it is largely untested whether this lets them learn a rule nobody told them. An agent can also pass by writing down each correction as an exception, and its list then grows with every new rule. We introduce CLR-Bench, a Curriculum of Latent Rules benchmark. Each chain adds one hidden rule per level on top of the earlier ones. A rule acts on an opaque label that stands for a named grouping published on the Web, such as the founding members of an airline alliance. The task gives one example value, practice feedback reveals one more member and one non-member, and the test checks unseen members and similar non-members. Probes certify that the base model knows the members of each grouping and does not guess it without feedback, and that the evidence identifies the grouping once labels are read as named groupings. An automated pipeline builds chains from a new data domain, and we release 20 chains over 10 domains. We evaluate six recent self-evolution methods. With the certifying model they barely learn. The best gain at most 5 points over a frozen agent and exclude only 6-12% of the unseen members from the count, fewer than the 20% reached by simply keeping the raw practice history. A fixed lesson that states the named-grouping convention lifts the same methods by 14.5 to 16.5 points. Their states hold the revealed member in 75-98% of cases and almost never the class name, and when practice exposes a member the list misses, they add that member to the list. With the stronger GPT-6-Sol, ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet learn from feedback alone. They reach 78% accuracy and solve 59-60% of the single cells, against 53% and 8% with the certifying model, and they surpass the raw history. CLR-Bench therefore measures how well an agent learns, and this ability differs across models.

title: Functional-Specific Information Borrowing under Limited Overlap
comment: 21 pages, 2 figures; complete proofs included. Supplement B is supplied as extracted ancillary files in anc/
summary: Source observations can improve a target average without estimating the entire shared response accurately. We study this distinction in two independent observational samples whose treatment effects share a rough component and differ by a smoother discrepancy. For power-law treatment overlap known for the analysis, known design density, fixed positive Sobolev radii, and Gaussian noise, we derive matching minimax mean squared error bounds with three regimes. Two explicit source-information thresholds determine the onset of rate improvement and attainment of the source-known rate. A signed local correction explains the thresholds: source observations estimate only the part of the integration functional poorly recovered from the target sample. Direct likelihood lower bounds apply to all estimators. Existing joint reproducing-kernel recovery, which does not require propensity inputs, attains these rates, and standard bias-aware intervals are conditionally honest under the specified class. A supplementary zero-overlap result separates estimation error from residual identification uncertainty. Numerical results illustrate both gains and losses when the total number of participants is fixed. The intermediate rate depends on overlap geometry, while smoothness determines its two endpoints.

title: Frequency-Calibrated Decision-Focused Learning for BESS Dispatch Under Renewable Uncertainty
summary: Battery energy storage system (BESS) flexibility depends on state of charge and intertemporal operating constraints. Renewable forecast errors of similar magnitudes can lead to different BESS dispatch results. An error may alter early charging or discharging decisions and reduce the flexibility available for subsequent regulation, while another may have little effect on the resulting schedule. To account for these unequal consequences, this paper proposes Frequency-Calibrated Decision-Focused Learning (FC-DFL), which trains renewable predictors using the realized operating costs of their induced BESS schedules. Gaussian smoothing and solver-based zeroth-order estimation provide training feedback without requiring differentiating through the non-differentiable mixed-integer BESS dispatch problem. The same decision feedback is further combined with prediction sensitivity to develop a decision-oriented XAI method that identifies the input features and forecast periods most consequential to BESS operation. Case studies using German wind and solar data show that FC-DFL reduces the integrated absolute frequency-deviation metric by 6.05% and decision regret by 23.92% relative to accuracy-based predict-then-optimize method. The XAI analysis further demonstrates that the identified high-impact forecast periods produce 2.84 times larger average absolute changes in realized operating cost than low-impact periods. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating downstream decision-making outcomes into renewable forecasting and demonstrate the value of FC-DFL in improving BESS regulation and providing operationally meaningful forecast explanations.

title: TAPE: Learning General Audio Effect Representations
comment: Submitted to Transactions of Machine Learning Research; 25 pages, 5 figures, 18 tables
summary: Musicians and mixing engineers often can decipher the signal processing chain they hear on a reference recording, then adapt it to new material. We present TAPE (Transformations of Audio Parameter Embeddings), which estimates this processing from the processed reference audio alone. An encoder trained to identify processors in eight major effect families maps the reference to an embedding. A differentiable digital signal processing (DSP) chain decodes the embedding into editable parameters in one forward pass and applies them to a different unprocessed recording. Its modules are equalization, compression, waveshaping, a small residual network, and reverberation. TAPE achieves lower spectral error than DeepAFx-ST, the previous state of the art for single-step regression, and lower spectral error than per-example search over a chain approximating ST-ITO's, while running 275$\times$ faster than that search. Because the decoder outputs DSP parameters, its chain can also run causally: a C++ implementation with the trained weights processed 128-sample buffers 1.8$\times$ faster than real time, with no missed deadlines.

title: Bethe Hessian Recovery through the Kesten-Stigum Regime
summary:
We show that outlier eigenvectors of the Bethe Hessian achieve weak recovery in the stochastic block model down to the Kesten-Stigum threshold, for every fixed common expected degree $d>1$. This extends previous recovery guarantees, which required $d$ to be sufficiently large. This threshold is information-theoretically optimal for the symmetric two-community model and is conjectured to mark the limit of efficient recovery in broader symmetric models. Our result matches the recovery guarantees of non-backtracking spectral methods while using Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices.
  To do this, we identify recursive formulas for the negative outlier eigenvalues and show that their eigenspaces have nonvanishing overlap with the corresponding planted eigenspaces. The proof constructs approximate eigenvectors from the planted labels on the limiting Poisson tree, with weights given by its Green's function, and transfers these approximations to the finite graph.

title: Downlink MU-MIMO for LEO Direct-to-Device: Feasibility, Architecture, and Implementation
summary: Direct-to-device connectivity from low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites is commercially available, but its throughput is limited by the satellite antenna size and by payloads that separate users only by beams and frequency reuse. This article shows that a single LEO satellite with a meter-scale array can serve hundreds of users on the same time-frequency resource through multi-user multiple-input multiple-output precoding. The number of users it can separate with a single stream each, i.e., its spatial degrees of freedom (DoF), follows from the aperture in wavelengths, the orbit altitude, and the minimum elevation angle. With minimum mean-square error (MMSE) precoding, the throughput of these users grows with the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), whereas maximum-ratio transmission becomes interference-limited. The precoder can be computed from the user positions and the satellite ephemeris and attitude, with a throughput loss of less than 0.5\% at 20~dB SNR compared with perfect channel knowledge under the 3GPP non-terrestrial channel models. The DoF also set the number of digital chains of a hybrid payload, and the functional split among satellites and ground trades inter-satellite-link and feeder-link load against on-board processing. As the satellite moves, the precoder can be updated from the known geometry every radio frame, i.e., 10~ms, while the computationally intensive user pairing can be kept for a few seconds with a throughput loss below 1\%. Finally, we keep the cell-specific signals on fixed beams while precoding the user data jointly across all cells of the satellite. For a $50\times50$ array at 600~km and a minimum elevation angle of $60^\circ$, one satellite serves 410 users at 6.1~bps/Hz on average, more than four times the throughput of fixed beams with four-color frequency reuse.

title: Personalised 3D Mnemonics for Vocabulary Learning in Context
summary: Augmented reality (AR) can support vocabulary learning by placing mnemonic cues in the physical contexts where new words are encountered. Prior work has augmented real objects with bilingual labels, audio, keywords, and 3D visualisations of those keywords interacting with the objects, but these cues are typically predefined by system designers. This limits scalability and reduces learners' ability to construct personal mnemonic links. By grounding mnemonics in objects that learners already recognise, use, and associate with prior experiences, a system could connect new vocabulary to existing mental models rather than requiring learners to adopt designer-defined associations. We outline a proof of concept and a storyboard of a generative AR approach in which learners create personalised 3D mnemonics by transforming familiar objects in their surroundings into situated mnemonic anchors. We position this concept within a timeline of related work and argue that recent advances in generative 3D asset creation enable a new design point: personalised 3D mnemonics that do not merely place content in the physical learning environment, but modify familiar real-world objects so that they become part of the mnemonic itself.

title: Observation-Specific Uncertainty Modeling for Latent-Variable Regression in High-Dimensional Analytical Data
comment: 42 pages including 14 pages of Supplementary Information; 9 main figures and 9 supplementary figures
summary: Across many fields, including medical diagnostics, process monitoring, and quality control, decisions often rely on point predictions for single samples. Observation-specific uncertainty is needed to assess the risk of decision error when predictions are compared with thresholds. Latent-variable regression is widely used for such predictions, but observation-specific uncertainty remains difficult to estimate. Traditional methods assume unbiased predictions, attributing prediction uncertainty solely to variance. However, dimensionality reduction can introduce observation-specific bias, violating this assumption. We introduce a framework using Gaussian processes trained on latent scores and prediction errors to estimate observation-specific bias and error variance, separating systematic error from epistemic and aleatoric variance. In Raman measurements of a fructose-sucrose model system, estimated prediction-error distributions agreed with empirical distributions; bias correction reduced mean squared error, and decision limits incorporating bias and variance improved analyte detection over variance-only limits. An aqueous-solubility application using molecular descriptors demonstrated the framework's generalisation beyond spectroscopy.

title: Multi-Timescale Deliverability of Shared Hybrid Storage for AI Data Center Campuses
summary: Artificial intelligence data center (AIDC) campuses contain sustained power variations and subsecond power fluctuations, requiring both sufficient stored energy and fast response. A shared hybrid energy storage system (HESS) can mitigate aggregate AIDC power deviations, but interval-based schedules cannot capture the delay between commanded and delivered power at the campus point of common coupling (PCC). To this end, this paper proposes a multi-timescale scheduling model for mitigating AIDC power fluctuations with the shared HESS. First, it models electrical pooling at the campus bus and constrains the shared HESS to a single PCC injection. Second, a two-layer model passes five-minute scheduled power, energy state, and reserve capacity to a causal fast response model that distinguishes commanded power from delivered power. Case studies using the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) GenAI Power Profiles Dataset show reductions in both PCC and fast integral absolute error (IAE), while retaining most of the improvement available under ideal response.

title: Retrieve-then-Disambiguate: Scalable Reviewer Discovery
summary: The growing number of scientific submissions is straining the peer review process, while a large pool of relevant researchers remains unidentified and is therefore not considered as potential reviewers. We formulate the discovery of these researchers as a retrieval problem: given a submission, we retrieve and rank researchers based on domain similarity. We present retrieve-then-disambiguate, an open-source algorithm that identifies domain relevant researchers for a query submission by retrieving similar publications from the scientific literature and resolving ambiguous author names into unique researcher identities. We evaluate the algorithm on 500 astronomy and physics publications. We use ORCID-linked first authors, coauthors, and cited researchers as proxy labels to evaluate the recovery of researchers with known connections to each query publication. When retrieving the top 500 most similar papers, the algorithm recovers roughly 68\% of first authors, 60\% of coauthors, and 45\% of cited researchers. Our code is available at https://github.com/deepthought-initiative/Retrieve-then-Disambiguate.

title: Improved estimation of differential entropy of a multivariate Gaussian distribution
summary: We consider estimation of entropy of a multivariate variate normal distribution with unknown mean vector and unknown covariance matrix. Using a decision-theoretic approach, we study the problem under a general location-invariant loss function that is strictly convex and minimized at zero. We first characterize the class of affine equivariant estimators and obtain the best affine equivariant estimator. We further show that the best affine equivariant estimator is inadmissible under the general loss. Exploiting information in the sample mean, we derive Stein-type improved estimators, including an extension to the case of a mean matrix. Under the linex loss, we obtain a smooth Brewster--Zidek-type estimator that dominates the best affine equivariant estimator, and we show that this estimator is generalized Bayes under a suitable non-informative prior.

title: PBSR: Pseudo-Burst Super-Resolution via Zero-Shot Novel View Synthesis
comment: Accepted for publication in New Generation Computing. 17 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables
summary: Burst super-resolution (BSR) achieves higher reconstruction fidelity than single-image super-resolution (SISR) by aggregating sub-pixel information from multiple frames. However, it requires a burst of frames captured under near-static conditions, and such frames are unavailable for single photographs or archival images. We propose Pseudo-Burst Super-Resolution (PBSR), which brings BSR-style reconstruction to the single-image input setting by synthesizing pseudo-burst frames via zero-shot novel view synthesis (NVS). PBSR first generates pseudo-burst frames with realistic parallax using a viewpoint sampling strategy calibrated to the pixel-shift distribution of real burst datasets. The frames are then processed by a BSR backbone equipped with a geometry-aware alignment module that reuses the NVS camera parameters and estimated depth. While the NVS stage is zero-shot, the backbone is fine-tuned with an artifact-aware adaptation so that it can exploit the synthesized frames despite their generative artifacts. Experiments on the BurstSR dataset show that PBSR consistently improves in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS over the single-frame baseline with the same reconstruction backbone.

title: Uniform Non-Deterministic Semantics for Ciuciura's $mbC^n$-Hierarchy
summary: We introduce a uniform non-deterministic semantics for the hierarchy of paraconsistent systems mbC^n introduced by Ciuciura. The proposed construction generalizes Omori's three-valued semantics for mbC^1 to all systems of the hierarchy. We prove soundness and completeness of the semantics with respect to the corresponding axiomatizations and show that the consequence relations of the systems mbC^n cannot be characterized by finite deterministic matrices.

title: Unifying Data-Adaptive Longitudinal Treatment-Effect Subgroup Discovery and Pretreatment Membership Prediction
summary: Precision medicine seeks to match patients with treatments from which they are most likely to benefit. A key step toward this goal is to learn treatment-effect heterogeneity from longitudinal study data. This requires discovering subgroups with distinct treatment-effect trajectories and predicting subgroup membership for new patients from pretreatment information. Existing methods do not fully unify these tasks. Covariate-informed membership models typically prespecify the subgroup number or covariance structure, whereas data-adaptive discovery methods often require prediction in a separate stage. We propose a data-adaptive semiparametric mixture-of-experts framework that unifies longitudinal treatment-effect subgroup discovery and pretreatment membership prediction. Subgroup-specific varying-coefficient functions characterize treatment-effect trajectories, while flexible covariance functions account for within-subject dependence. A covariate-dependent gating model links membership to pretreatment characteristics. A penalty on global component weights removes redundant subgroups, while separate gating coefficients allow patient-specific membership probabilities among retained subgroups. A blockwise generalized expectation--maximization algorithm estimates all model components under a single penalized observed-data objective. We establish consistent subgroup-number selection, convergence rates for the functional estimators, and asymptotic normality for the finite-dimensional parameters. Simulations show reliable subgroup-number selection and more accurate conditional membership prediction than a two-step procedure. Applications to the SANAD epilepsy study and the COMPETE migraine trial identify distinct temporal treatment-effect patterns.

title: With foundation-model features, aggregator complexity does not improve cross-hospital discrimination in gastric whole-slide image classification
summary: Whole-slide image classifiers are usually developed within one hospital and often go untested at unseen hospitals. We assembled 5,036 haematoxylin-and-eosin-stained gastric slides from five Korean hospitals, scanned at 20x and 40x, and compared multiple-instance learning aggregators under leave-one-hospital-out validation on frozen pathology foundation-model features. A hierarchical patch-region-slide graph aggregator (CHIME-MIL) with site alignment and two-scale fusion reached a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.837, above six conventional attention and transformer aggregators trained without these steps. Under a matched recipe it did not exceed attention-based pooling, and global max pooling given the same alignment and fusion was better (AUC 0.855, P = 0.0002). The alignment, which subtracts each hospital's mean feature vector without labels, onboarded a new hospital from ten unlabelled slides and cost 0.002 AUC without held-out-hospital data, but its accuracy gains were small and inconsistent. The model had low top-label calibration error (0.053) but under-confident malignancy probabilities, and removing its most-attended patches lowered the malignancy probability far more than removing random patches. With these features, more complex aggregators did not improve discrimination; what a deployable system adds is label-free onboarding, calibration checks and auditable evidence.

title: Beyond Plausible Prediction: Safety Sufficiency in Web World Models
summary: Web world models increasingly predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, yet a plausible predicted future does not necessarily support the correct safety decision. In a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. However, several models exhibit highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour, combining low false-safe execution with poor recall of clarifiable ASK cases and a strong preference for BLOCK. This motivates safety sufficiency: whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required to distinguish actions that may be EXECUTED, require clarification through ASK, or should be BLOCKED. We introduce SafeWebWorld, a benchmark for evaluating safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains through action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions. Under a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol, evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. To determine whether this deterioration reflects loss of authorisation-sensitive score structure or a failure of the decision readout, we introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR). Frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, while paired recovery provides only a modest additional gain. Yet within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor, showing that aggregate recoverability does not imply robust fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Overall, plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recovery are each insufficient on their own to establish robust authorisation.

title: Statistical Foundations of Reinforcement Learning: A Non-Asymptotic Perspective
summary:
Reinforcement learning (RL) embodies a foundational paradigm for sequential decision-making in the face of uncertainty. The rapid growth of model complexity in emerging applications has significantly amplified the challenges of achieving data-efficient RL, particularly in sample-starved scenarios where data collection may be costly, time-consuming, or even high-stakes. Consequently, understanding and improving the data efficiency of RL algorithms has become a central problem of both fundamental theoretical interest and practical importance.
  Despite decades of research, the statistical underpinnings of RL remained remarkably underdeveloped until relatively recently, particularly in the finite-sample regimes most relevant to modern practice. Over the past few years, there has been a surge of activity advancing the frontiers of non-asymptotic statistical RL theory, drawing on ideas from high-dimensional statistics and probability, information theory, and statistical learning theory. In this monograph, we present a non-asymptotic treatment for RL based on tabular Markov decision processes, focusing on three canonical sampling mechanisms --- RL with a generative model, online RL, and offline RL --- together with two algorithmic paradigms: model-based and model-free approaches. Centered around non-asymptotic sample complexity analysis, our treatment emphasizes minimax-optimal algorithm design, particularly methods that attain statistical optimality without significant burn-in costs, as well as sharp statistical characterizations of several widely used RL algorithms. Whenever possible, we provide largely self-contained analyses together with intuitive explanations. We also briefly discuss several extensions, such as robust RL, competitive multi-agent RL, federated RL, uncertainty quantification, and RL from human feedback.

title: Bayesian PET Reconstruction with Learned Flow Matching Priors via Langevin Sampling
comment: Selected as the Best Student Paper Award for 2026 IVMSP
summary: Image reconstruction for positron emission tomography (PET) is a challenging inverse problem due to its inherent ill-posedness and Poisson counting noise, particularly in low-dose acquisitions. In this work, we introduce a novel Bayesian PET reconstruction framework that leverages a flow-matching generative prior learned from high-quality PET images. By incorporating this prior, we formulate PET reconstruction as a Bayesian inference problem and solve it via latent-space posterior sampling using the unadjusted Langevin algorithm. We evaluate the proposed method through numerical experiments and benchmark it against classical reconstruction methods and state-of-the-art deep learning-based baselines. The proposed method achieves improved reconstruction performance while enabling posterior uncertainty quantification.

title: CaPtain: A Pipeline for Post-Training Code-as-Policy Robot Agents
summary: Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it. Code-as-policy (CaP) casts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply. Yet existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware. We first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, then apply multi-turn RL. Multi-turn RL must credit tens of agent requests, whose physical effects often surface turns later, from a single end-of-episode outcome. We therefore introduce a physical critic that reads privileged simulator state, never seen by the policy, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success. Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B reaches 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points). Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation. We release all code, data, and model weights.

title: Parametric inference for the average hazard approach in time-to-event analysis with sparse risk sets
summary: The average hazard (AH) is a recently proposed model-free summary of an event-time distribution. Over a prespecified window $[0,τ]$, it equals the cumulative incidence probability at $τ$ divided by the restricted mean survival time at $τ$ and can be interpreted as a person-time incidence rate that does not depend on the censoring distribution. The difference and ratio of AHs from two groups, DAH and RAH, are between-group contrasts on absolute and relative scales without requiring proportional hazards. Existing nonparametric inference for AH and its contrasts is based on the Kaplan--Meier estimator of the survival function, and can become unreliable when risk sets become sparse or exhausted near $τ$, as may occur in stratified analyses.
